lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A patient presents with congestive heart failure, widespread edema (anasarca). Their measured serum Na is low. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: The low serum Na indicates a water handling problem and has nothing to say about total body sodium
This patient has far too much sodium. The edema and CHF indicate very high total body sodium
The low serum Na is not an indicator of some sort of sodium deficit and giving this patient more sodium would be dangerous

answer:
The correct answer is D.

All 3 are correct. Measured serum Na is a cheap, readily available and (usually) accurate surrogate for serum Osm. It is absolutely not any indication of the total body sodium of the patient. Total body sodium is a clinical assessment. If the ECF volume is clearly expanded, then the patient has too much sodium and needs to get rid of it

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following are non-osmotic stimuli for the release of ADH?

options.html: Drugs that block the RAAS (eg ACEI)

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, D.

By taking over from our brains chemoreceptors, these conditions can cause us to retain free water, even if it means dropping our osmolality and causing cell swelling. While mild ECFV contraction usually has a minimal effect, it can become a very potent stimulus for ADH release through stimulation of the RAAS system.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: In a patient with high serum potassium, which one statement is FALSE?

options.html: Their aldosterone level should rise to help respond
The overwhelming mortality of daily potassium excretion takes place by the kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This is false. If all the “machinery” is working properly, high K is sensed, adrenals kick into action releasing aldosterone, kidneys are the main conduit for K out of the body. In the presence of high aldosterone, the CCD should be able to maintain a high urinary K and thus a high gradient, and the TTKG should be >7, not <2.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following suggests inappropriate renal losses of K in a patient with hypokalemia (choose all that are correct)

options.html: 24h urine collection shows 50 mmol of K

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, D.

Spot urine [K] of 45 is very high. If the serum K is low the body should try to get the urine K as low as possible. A high urine K suggests the kidneys are likely at fault. Nonanion gap metabolic acidosis. While this may go along with renal causes, it can also accompany GI causes so this is incorrect. Calculated TTKG of 11. This is also very high (see A above) 24h urine collection shows 50 mmol of K. this is very high (see A above).

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: For the emergency treatment of hyperkalemia, which of the following is true? Choose all that are correct

options.html: Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride IV will quickly lower the potassium to safe levels
Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride IV will help prevent or stop heart rhythm problems
Insulin will shift potassium into cells, quickly lowering it to safe levels
Potassium may shift back out after any acute treatment, so efforts to enhance elimination are important

answer:
The correct answer is B, C, D, E.

All are correct except A.IV calcium salts antagonize the cardiotoxicity of hyperkalemia by stabilizing the cardiac cell membrane against undesirable depolarization, but they don’t change the measured level of potassium.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Adrianus’ grandparents are visiting from the Netherlands. They brough a big bag of black licorice and he has been eating it for a week. He feels unwell with headaches and weakness. Which of the following is/are true of excess mineralocorticoid (pick all that are correct).

options.html: This ABG is compatible: pH 7.49, bicarb 35, pCO2 47
Excess activity in CCD causes both excessive potassium and hydrogen (ammonium) loss causing hypokalemia and alkalosis together

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C.

The licorice contains an ingredient that interferes with normal mineralocorticoid metabolism, leading to excess activity which mimics hyperaldosteronism. His ABG shows chronic metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory response. High aldosterone-like activity causes sodium retention and high BP, while wasting potassium and hydrogen

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Imagine a performance athlete running a marathon on a hot day. Along the way they are sweating profusely, but they grab a glass of water at each aid station to make sure they are staying “well hydrated”. Which of the following is/are true (select all that apply).

options.html: Drinking lots of water will help to maintain the ECF volume
As they sweat and lose fluids along the way, the RAAS system will be stimulated, leading in turn to elevated ADH which helps to retain the consumed water
This is a high risk situation that can lead to seizures or even death

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

The runner has lost salt water, and total body sodium is low. They need electrolytes to replenish the ECF. Electrolyte free water distributes 2/3 to the ICF. The low ECF does stimulate ADH. If they are consuming electrolyte free water, this will be retained even as the serum Na (and Osm) are falling, and cells are swelling. Every year people die running marathons, as the result of exercise induced hyponatremia. They do not understand the need to eat salty snacks and drink electrolytes, not just drink copious water.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 37 year old woman who is 6 weeks postpartum presents to her family physician with complaints of severe pain. It started in her back on the right side, moved to her right flank, and is now in her right inguinal region. Which of the following could explain her current inguinal pain?

options.html: Visceral Afferents travelling from the kidneys to spinal level T10
Visceral Afferents travelling from the proximal ureter to spinal level T11
Visceral Afferents travelling from the distal ureter to spinal level L1

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The inguinal region is located around dermatome L1 and visceral afferents from the distal ureter would be sent to this spinal level.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following best describes the relationships of the RIGHT adrenal gland? (Select All That Apply)

options.html: Separated from Kidney by Renal Fascia

answer:
The correct answer is B, C, D, E.

The right adrenal gland is superior to the right kidney separated by a thin layer of renal fascia. Both the kidney and the adrenal gland are surrounded by pararenal fat, which acts to hold it in place. The right adrenal gland is inferior to the intraperitoneal liver, but it itself is retroperitoneal along with the kidneys. The medial aspect of the adrenal gland is closely associated with the retroperitoneal IVC.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The renal system does NOT play a direct role in regulating which one of the following?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The kidneys are vital in maintaining blood pressure, blood pH and blood solute concentrations. They do not have a significant role in temperature regulation.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following anatomical portion of a nephron connects the Bowman’s capsule to the loop of Henle?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Bowmans capsule joins the proximal convoluted tubule which takes the glomerular filtrate to the Loop of Henle.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The glomerular filtration barrier is composed of all of the following except:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The Macula densa is a special group of cells that senses the ionic content of the urine but DOES NOT form a component of the glomerular filtration barrier.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: If a patient is volume overloaded, and has elevated hydrostatic pressure in their capillaries, what would Starling Forces do with that extra fluid?

options.html: Cause fluid to leave the capillaries into the interstitium?
Cause a fluid buildup inside the capillaries leading to hypertension?

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A is correct. Starling Forces would tend to push the fluid into the interstitium. It is true that the patient would tend to be hypertensive in an overloaded state, but this is not because of Starling Forces.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: If a patient had a kidney stone blocking the drainage of urine and increasing pressure in the urinary tubules what would happen to the GFR in the affected kidney?

options.html: The Starling Force of hydrostatic force in Bowman’s space would push back against filtration, and hence lower the GFR
The Starling Force of hydrostatic force in Bowman’s space would decrease, allowing for more filtration and increase the GFR

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A is correct, the GFR would go down (see image below as well).

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: In acute ischemic injury of the kidney, the polarity of tubular cells is lost. The main problem of this would be:

options.html: Failure to maintain proper gradients of low intracellular Na allowing unidirectional movement of Na

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The answer is B. The loss of polarity means that tubular cells are no longer moving filtered Na from the urine back into the interstitium. The low intracellular Na and location of Na/K ATPase on the basolateral membrane insures unidirectional movement of Na (and a lot of transporters are linked to this).

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A drug that blocks the actions of the Principal cell will cause high blood potassium (hyperkalemia) and low blood pH (metabolic acidosis) by interfering with both Principal cell and a-Intercalated cell. Is this statement True or False?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The answer is true. Drugs such as spironolactone or amiloride prevent the Principal cell from working. This blocks K secretion but also prevents the lumen from becoming negative, necessary for proton pump by adjacent a-Intercalated cell. As a result, potassium accumulates in the blood (hyperkalemia) and the kidney fails to get rid of acid (acidosis).

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Patients taking diuretics acting in the loop of Henle (“loop diuretics” e.g. furosemide) have difficulties with both concentrating and diluting their urine. Their urine Osm is often close to serum Osm (in the 250-400 mOsm/L) range. Which points are correct in these patients? (Select all that apply).

options.html: The urine leaving the TAL has an Osm of around 50 mOsm/L
The urine concentration is limited because of a lack of solute in the medullary interstitium
The urine entering the proximal tubule has an Osm of around 300 mOsm/L

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

Because TAL can’t extract solute, the urine heading into the DCT is not very dilute, so A is incorrect. Urine entering the proximal tubule is always similar to serum Osm, so C is correct (and not particularly relevant to the question). The lack of active transport of solute into the medulla means there is a lack of interstitial solute to draw water out of the collecting duct in response to ADH, so B is

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Patients taking thiazides acting in the DCT have difficulties with diluting their urine. Which points are correct in these patients? (Select all that apply).

options.html: The urine leaving the DCT has an Osm of around 50 mOsm/L
The countercurrent multiplier is working leading to the presence of solute in the medullary interstitium
Volume contraction stimulates RAAS and ADH which causes reabsorption of water by the collecting duct, and a high urine Osm

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

Because DCT can’t extract solute, the urine heading out of the DCT is not as dilute as it should be, so A is incorrect. Because the TAL is working fine, active transport of solute into the medulla means there is plenty of interstitial solute by the countercurrent multiplier, so B is correct. ECF volume contraction is a potent stimulus for RAAS and ADH, and because B is correct, there is lots of solute to draw water out of the collecting duct in response to ADH, so C is correct.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Sodium is always trying to move from the ultrafiltrate/urine to the interstitium. Which of the following are true?

options.html: Na/K-ATPase maintains a high intracellular Na along the nephron, which provides a gradient from the cells into the interstitium
Na only moves with a corresponding anion to maintain electrical neutrality
We reabsorb less than half of the daily filtered Na
None of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is D.

None of these are true! Na/K-ATPase maintains a low, not high, intracellular Na along the nephron, provides gradient from the urine into the cells, and ATPase moves it to interstitium. Na moves down its gradient with anions, but also can move in exchange for cations. We typically reabsorb ~99% of our daily filtered Na; if we lost half of the filtered Na, we would quickly drop dead from ECF volume contraction.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Why do we try to reabsorb almost all of our filtered sodium? Which of these are true?

options.html: Na is the predominant cation of the ECF, so the amount of Na needs to be carefully regulated to keep our BP and tissue perfusion at adequate levels
Na transporters (antiporters and cotransporters) enable the kidney to carefully balance other electrolytes, pH and secrete wastes
Removing Na from the ultrafiltrate enables us to pee out a very dilute urine if ADH is suppressed (in times of water excess)
Packing sodium into the medullary interstitium enables us to pee out a very concentrated urine if ADH is activated (in times of water deprivation)
None of the above are true.

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D.

Na/K-ATPase keeps almost all of our Na in the ECF space, so the total amount of Na (not the concentration) determines our ECF and is carefully regulated. Na transporters help the kidney in its role as the “master chemist” of the body. Intact Na handling enables the countercurrent mechanism to work properly, helping us to respond to presence or absence of ADH. So diuretics which “poison” the Na transporters mess up our ability to dilute and concentrate the urine normally. They also make us “pee out salt”, and hence lower the ECF volume.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Andrew had a weekend of very high salt intake. He had pizza one night, was snacking on peanuts and salty chips, and the next day had bacon and eggs. For fun, someone measured his plasma Na which was normal here. Which of the following statements are true (select all that apply?)

options.html: Andrew’s total body Na is high, irrespective of his measured [Na] in the plasma
Andrew’s RAAS system is suppressed, and his urine Na is high as he tries to return his ECF back down to normal
Andrew’s aldosterone is elevated, causing him to retain all of the dietary sodium

answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

C. Andrew’s total body Na is high, his ECF is expanded. He has too much salt. This made him thirsty so he drank enough water to keep his serum Na at a normal level. The expanded ECF was sensed by multiple sensors, and his RAAS is inhibited, in order to help him pee out sodium and restore his ECF. RAAS includes aldosterone, so his aldosterone should also be suppressed to pee out sodium.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A patient presents with hypertension and a tumor of the adrenal gland which autonomously secretes high levels of aldosterone. Which are correct (select all that appy)?

options.html: The high level of aldosterone causes excess uptake of Na mostly by the distal convoluted tubular cell
Sodium retention and high BP cause ECF sensors to shut down renin and angiotensin production and release, but the high aldosterone persists
Excess activity of the principal cell of the distal convoluted tubule causes excessive potassium secretion, as well as increased acid secretion by the adjacent ⍺-intercalated cells

answer:
The correct answer is B.

This tumor and this clinical scenario is called “Conn’s syndrome”. B is the only correct answer. Sodium retention and high BP cause ECF sensors to shut down renin and angiotensin production and release, but the high aldosterone persists. The diagnosis is suggested by very high levels of the aldosterone/renin ratio. A and C sound correct, but the primary site of action of aldosterone and the location of the principal and ⍺-intercalated cells is the collecting duct, not the DCT.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: In a patient with recently discovered renal failure, the most appropriate initial imaging study would be:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

You always need to rule out post renal causes of acute kidney injury. If a renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, This needs to be corrected urgently.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 70 year old male is admitted to hospital after developing a flu-like illness associated with diarrhea and vomiting. The urea (BUN) is 16 mmol/L (normal 3-6); the serum creatinine is 120 µmol/L (normal up to 100 µmol/L). From this data, you would conclude:

options.html: The patient is developing urinary tract obstruction
The patient likely has acute tubular necrosis
The patient’s symptoms are likely due to chronic renal failure
The patient is probably volume depleted
The patient is developing post-infectious glomerulonephritis

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The blood urea to creatinine ratio is 16000/100 which is 160. This is much higher than 80 and points to a pre-renal cause of acute kidney injury.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 45 year old patient is admitted to hospital with joint pain and a diffuse maculopapular rash 3 days after being initiated on penicillin for Group A streptococcus pharyngitis. Blood work reveals an elevated serum creatinine of 200 umol/L and urinalysis reveals 3+ leukocytes, 1+ blood, trace protein. Urine microscopy reveals WBC casts. The most likely diagnosis for this patients acute kidney injury is:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

The pyuria and white blood cell casts clearly indicate the presence of acute interstitial nephritis. Antibiotics are a common cause of acute kidney injury from acute interstitial nephritis.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the conditions is most likely to present with rapidly worsening renal function and red cell casts in the urine:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (formerly Wegeners Granulomatosis), microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as ChurgStrauss) and the common diseases that can cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following urinary findings is most suggestive of “pre-renal” acute renal failure from volume contraction rather than acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

When you are in a pre-renal state like volume contraction, you turn on renin-angiotensin aldosterone system but you also turn on ADH which makes you reabsorb water at the level of the collecting tubule. This concentrates your urine and gives you a high urine osmolality.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 45 year old man presents to your clinic with advanced renal failure and a serum creatinine of 200 µmol/L. Renal ultrasound reveals enlarged kidneys bilaterally measuring 20 cm in size with multiple bilateral renal cysts.
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Polycystic kidney disease is the most common genetic cause of end stage renal disease and is associated with enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The commonest cause of chronic kidney disease in an adult in Canada is:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Diabetes Mellitus is by far the most common cause of end stage renal disease in the world.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Regarding Chronic Kidney Disease Stage IV, which of the following is true:

options.html: It is defined as an eGFR < 45 ml/min
Most patients with this condition will eventually require renal replacement therapy
The commonest cause of death in these patients is cardiovascular disease
Patients with proteinuria are less likely to progress to end-stage renal failure
The commonest cause of CKD Stage IV in Canada is glomerulonephritis

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Kidney disease is often a marker of vascular disease elsewhere in the body. Kidney patients also have several risk factors for progressive cardiovascular disease.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 40 year old Type II diabetic male with a serum creatinine of 200, inadequately controlled hypertension and proteinuria is started on an ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker); Which of the following tests is highest priority to order within 2 weeks?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

In patients with low GFR, ACE inhibitors make you more prone to hyperkalemia, so it is important to check your electrolytes 2 weeks after starting an ACE-inhibitor. It is normal for the serum creatinine to go up by 20% after starting an ACE inhibitor but this will preserve the kidney function over a prolonged period of time. If the serum creatinine goes up by more than that, than you have to consider bilateral renal artery stenosis and the ACE inhibitor may need to be stopped as the intraglomerular pressure has gone too low.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following regarding the use of ACE inhibitors in diabetic nephropathy is correct?

options.html: Should be initiated once microalbuminuria is persistent even if the patient is normotensive
Causes a rise in serum potassium only in patients with advanced renal failure
Precipitates acute gout in up to 5% of patients
Is contraindicated in patients with chronic obstructive airways disease
Often makes blood glucose control worse

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Persistent microalbuminuria indicates early diabetic nephropathy and these patients benefit from the initiation of ACE inhibitors in term of preventing progression to more advanced Chronic kidney disease.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following interventions is most important in a 50 year old man with Type II diabetes, a serum creatinine of 200 µmol/L, blood pressure of 180/100, and 2 grams of proteinuria daily:

options.html: Aggressive control of his hypertension with an ACE-inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker
Tightening of his blood sugar control

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Aggressive blood pressure control using ACE inhibitors as your first choice of agent is the most powerful thing you can do to slow down progression of chronic kidney disease.

Inflammation from the appendix spread to the Psoas investing fascia and the active contraction and passive stretch of the muscle resulted in pain.
The movement of the right thigh compresses the appendix in the abdomen resulting in pain

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Glucosuria is usually a sign of hyperglycemia from diabetes mellitus but could also represent dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule sodium glucose co transporter.

options.html: a decrease in the concentration of plasma protein
a decrease in renal blood flow

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Anything that increases intra glomerular pressure will increase GFR. Efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction does this.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease

stem: What is approximately the normal GFR in a young 70 kg adult male:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Normal GFR is adults ranges between 100 and 120 ml/min. It does does start to slowly decline naturally after the age of 40 by approximately 0.7 to 1 ml/min per year.

options.html: Formula using age, weight and gender

answer:
The correct answer is B.

CKD-EPI is where it is at. MDRD usually underestimates kidney function and Cockcroft Gault is just very inaccurate.

answer:

answer:

stem: As part of a physical exam for UDT, all of the following areas should be examined (select all that apply):
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, E.

A true UDT may be inside the abdomen or within the inguinal and suprascrotal space. Ectopic UDT may be present in the prepenile, femoral, perineal and transverse scrotal (the other scrotum). It is not found in the gluteal area.

All of these are scenarios for a non-palpable UDT. All of these scenarios require a diagnostic laparoscopy to determine. A peeping testicle can sometimes not be felt on physical exam; the same is true for an atrophic testis in the inguinal or scrotal region. In these scenarios, a diagnostic laparoscopy will help with diagnosing these.

In children with bilateral non-palpable UDT with either normal male genitalia or an ambiguous genitalia requires further workup to rule out endocrine abnormalities such as CAH. This includes a pelvic US, karyotype, MIS and a referral to endocrinology.

stem: A 12 year old boy presents to the ED with 6 hours of scrotal pain and swelling. He denies any nausea and vomiting. This started 2 days ago with an ache. He does not have fevers or any urinary symptoms. What is the next step?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient has a gradual onset of pain without nausea and vomiting makes testicular torsion less likely. The lack of fever and urinary symptoms makes epididymo-orchitis less likely. As such a urinalysis and culture will not be the first step. It is too early to consult Urology and we are not 100% sure that it is not testicular torsion. Therefore, the safest first step is to order a doppler ultrasound of the scrotum.

stem: Which of the following case scenarios would be more concerning for an anatomical or neurological cause for a child's enuresis (urinary incontinence) (select all that apply):
answer:
The correct answer is A, D, E.

In isolated day-time or isolated night-time enuresis, the probability of a neurological or anatomical cause is lower. This is because there is still bladder control. If there is an anatomical cause (i.e. stricture or physical obstruction), the child will have overflow incontinence, which is not restricted to day or night. If the cause is neurological, either overflow incontinence, bladder overactivity or even in a decompensated bladder (inability of bladder to contract), the symptoms will not be purely isolated to the day or night. Conversely, mixed enuresis, either primary and refractory to treatment or secondary mixed enuresis have a higher likelihood for an anatomical or neurological cause. True continuous incontinence (leaky faucet) can indicate an ectopic ureteric insertion from a duplicated kidney.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy

stem: You see a 6 year old female who has secondary daytime enuresis. She is dry at night. There is no history of urinary tract infection. She has a history of constipation, which is now controlled with PEG3350. A kidney bladder ultrasound was ordered and was normal. A voiding diary was completed, which showed a functional bladder capacity of 240 cc. She voids 2 times a day, which are both associated with significant urgency. She drinks around 6 cups of water per day. Upon interviewing the mother, she tells you that the urinary incontinence occurs when she rushes to the bathroom. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The child has elements of dysfunctional voiding, more specifically urinary postponement. The daytime enuresis is associated with urgency. She would benefit from timed voiding to ensure that she does not reach her maximum bladder capacity. She has a normal bladder capacity, so anticholinergic has no role. She is not constipated. She drinks a sufficient amount of water. She has a normal renal bladder ultrasound and isolated daytime incontinence, as such an anatomical or neurological cause is less likely; and conservative measures should be trialed prior to referral.

stem: Internalized ureteral stent failure is more common in patients with:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Ureteral stenting may not be as effective for treating patients with extrinsic ureteral obstruction. Docimo and Dewolf (1989) reported a mean 43% failure rate in ureteral stents placed for extrinsic ureteral obstruction, the majority related to malignancy. The association of stent failure and poor renal function has been reported by others (McCullough et al, 2008). The presence of extrinsic ureteral obstruction due to bladder or prostatic pathology, especially advanced malignancies, is another risk factor for stent failure (Danilovic et al, 2005).

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of these predict poor functional recovery after relief of ureteral obstruction?

options.html: Good compliance of the collecting system

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Factors that have a positive influence on functional recovery include a smaller degree of obstruction, greater compliance of the collecting system, and presence of pyelolymphatic backflow (Shokeir et al, 2002). Conversely, older age and decreased renal cortical thickness are predictors of diminished recovery of renal function (Lutaif et al, 2003).

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Ureteral stenting is preferred over percutaneous nephrostomy in patients with:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

If the patient with obstructive uropathy has an uncorrectable coagulopathy or platelet abnormality, ureteral stenting is indicated. Compared with percutaneous nephrostomy placement, stent insertion may require greater x-ray exposure (Mokhmalji et al, 2001). This may be of concern in pregnant patients, particularly early in gestation when the fetus is most sensitive to radiation effects (McAleer and Loughlin, 2004). Percutaneous nephrostomy should be strongly considered if pyonephrosis is suspected.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Postobstructive diuresis is:

options.html: common with unilateral obstruction in a patient with two kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Postobstructive diuresis is generally self-limited and is generally associated with initial hyposthenuric urine. Release of obstruction can result in marked diuresis and natriuresis.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The release of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) in obstructive uropathy is stimulated by:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The release of TNF-α, a potent inflammatory cytokine, is stimulated by angiotensin, especially in the first few hours of renal obstruction. It can upregulate its own expression as well as that of other inflammatory mediators, such as interleukin-1, platelet-activating factor, nitric oxide, eicosanoids, and cell adhesion molecules.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following characterizes obstructive nephropathy when compared to hydronephrosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The term obstructive nephropathy should be reserved for the damage to the renal parenchyma that results from an obstruction to the flow of urine anywhere along the urinary tract. The term hydronephrosis implies dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces and can occur without obstruction.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of these urinary changes occur after relief of bilateral ureteral obstruction?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

There is a profound increase in sodium excretion after relief of bilateral ureteral obstruction. This is due to ANP and perhaps reduced sodium transporters. The massive natriuresis enhances excretion of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following is thought to play a role in postobstructive diuresis after release of bilateral ureteral obstruction?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The accumulation of extracellular volume stimulates the synthesis and release of ANP, which promotes increased GFR and sodium excretion. Decreases in the aquaporin water channels in the kidney further promote the diuresis.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: After 5 hours of unilateral ureteral obstruction, which of the following occurs in the obstructed kidney?

options.html: Shift of blood flow from the outer to the inner cortex
Increased sodium delivery to the macula densa
Decrease in renal vein renin levels

answer:
The correct answer is C.

There is a shift of blood flow from the outer to inner cortex with UUO that is opposite to that which is seen with BUO. At the 5-hour interval of UUO, there is a reduction in renal plasma flow and GFR that results in diminished sodium delivery to the macula densa.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following occurs after bilateral ureteral obstruction?

options.html: Shift of blood flow to the outer renal cortex
Decrease in collecting system pressure during the first day
Increase in renal plasma flow at 8 hours

answer:
The correct answer is A.

There is a shift of blood flow to the outer renal cortex with BUO in contrast to the reversed pattern with UUO.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The chance for renal recovery after ureteral obstruction is most influenced by:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Although the other distractors influence recovery of renal function after release of obstruction, prompt eradication of obstruction provides the best approach for salvage.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following is expected in a kidney that has been obstructed for 1 month?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Obstruction results in a reduction in sodium transporters, including Na+, K+-ATPase. It also promotes tubulointerstitial fibrosis, reduction in aquaporin channels, and acidification defects. The collecting system pressure should not be increased at this point.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A reduction in concentrating ability of the obstructed kidney is due to:

options.html: maintenance of a medullary hypertonicity and reduced glomerular flow rate (GFR)
urea backflux from the inner medullary collecting duct

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The concentrating defect that occurs with obstruction is not due to inadequate levels of ADH. Choices b, c, and e result in enhanced concentrating ability, whereas a reduction in aquaporin-2 water channels does the opposite.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A persistent concentrating defect after relief of bilateral ureteral obstruction (BUO) is primarily due to:

options.html: continued excessive secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide
decreased release of ADH from the posterior pituitary

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Li and coworkers (2001) showed that the polyuria after release of BUO correlated with a decreased expression of aquaporins 1, 2, and 3. Over a 30-day period, the expressions of AQP-2 and -3 gradually normalized, but the expression of AQP-1 remained decreased. The reduced rate of synthesis and mobilization of water channels into the nephron membranes accounts for a decreased response to exogenous vasopressin or cyclic AMP.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: In studies of complete UUO for 24 hours, renal blood flow has been shown to:

options.html: briefly cease with ureteral clamping and then gradually return toward control
gradually decline over the course of the constriction
increase by 25% and remain elevated during the obstruction
increase over an hour and then steadily decrease
remain unchanged during clamping and undergo reactive hyperemia upon release

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Renal blood flow initially rises in the first phase, because of afferent arteriolar vasodilatation. In phase 2, efferent arteriolar constriction keeps ureteral pressure elevated, but in phase 3, both preglomerular and postglomerular vasoconstriction reduces renal blood flow and ureteral pressure.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Ureteral and tubular pressure changes in experimental unilateral ureteral occlusion over 24 hours are characterized by:

options.html: a continued increase due to urine secretion
an immediate decrease as flow ceases
an increase followed by a decrease
no change due to extravasation of tubule fluid
no change due to contralateral renal compensation

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The first phase is characterized by a rise in both ureteral pressure and renal blood flow lasting 1 to 1.5 hours. This is followed by a decline in renal blood flow (RBF) and a continued increase in ureteral (tubular) pressure lasting until the 5th hour of occlusion. The final phase involves a further decline in RBF and a progressive decline in ureteral pressure.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following have been implicated in the initial rise in renal blood flow in UUO?

options.html: Atrial natriuretic peptide and platelet-activating factor

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Studies during the early, vasodilatory phase of UUO have shown that the increase in RBF can be prevented by prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors, such as indomethacin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Intravenous administration of indomethacin before ureteral ligation results in a decline in renal blood flow without the initial vasodilatation. In addition, administration of nitric oxide (NO) synthesis inhibitors, such as N-nitro-l-arginine methyl ester (l-NAME) or N-monomethyl-l-arginine (l-NMMA), attenuates the initial rise in RBF with occlusion in rats, and when l-NMMA was discontinued, the rise in RBF was restored in 10 minutes. These findings provide evidence for a role of prostaglandins and nitric oxide in reducing preglomerular afferent arteriolar vascular resistance in the early phase of UUO.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 40-year-old man has anorexia, fatigue, and a serum creatinine value of 4.6 mg/dL. CT reveals severe bilateral hydronephrosis and a retroperitoneal soft tissue mass encasing the great vessels and ureters. The next step is:

options.html: open surgical biopsy of the mass

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In the acutely ill patient, initial therapy should be directed at draining the obstructed kidneys. Biopsy should be undertaken after metabolic stabilization. An underlying malignancy may be present in 8% to 10% of cases of suspected retroperitoneal fibrosis. This is most commonly obtained percutaneously, but open surgical biopsy may be necessary. Definitive therapy of retroperitoneal fibrosis, whether medical or surgical, should be delayed until after adequate drainage has been obtained and malignancy has been excluded.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers attenuate the decrease in GFR caused by ureteral obstruction by reducing constriction at which level?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Reduced preglomerular resistance increases glomerular capillary pressure and filtration rate.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Post-obstructive diuresis and natriuresis is seen more often following relief of BUO rather than UUO because:

options.html: renal sodium transporters are decreased only during BUO
third-space sequestration of fluid is greater with UUO
atrial natriuretic peptide secretion decreases during UUO
contralateral increases in transporters attenuates natriuresis of UUO
greater increases in vasopressin (ADH) with BUO inhibit sodium transport

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Diuresis and natriuresis occurs primarily after release of BUO because volume expansion, release of ANP, and decreases in the tubular sodium transporters all occur. With UUO, transporter synthesis increases in the unobstructed kidney to help compensate and reduce excretory losses in the obstructed kidney.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: What is the most common cause of gross prot in a patient older than 50 years of age?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The most common cause of gross hematuria in a patient older than age 50 years is bladder cancer.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: What is the most common cause of pain associated with gross hematuria?

options.html: Simultaneous passage of a kidney stone
Ureteral obstruction due to blood clots

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Pain in association with hematuria usually results from upper urinary tract hematuria with obstruction of the ureters with clots.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: All of the following are typical lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia EXCEPT:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Dysuria is painful urination that is usually caused by inflammation.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which statement is correct regarding the role of androgenic hormones in the etiology of BPH?

options.html: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone are the sole causes of the hyperplasia taking place in the prostate after the age of 40 years
The volume of androgen receptors in the prostate decreases with aging, leading to a lesser response to androgenic stimuli
Dihydrotestosterone is considered the more potent of the androgenic steroid hormones by a factor of approximately 10 : 1
Of the two 5α-reductase isoforms, type 1 is most commonly found in the prostate
Only testosterone produced in the testis and not in the adrenal gland enters into the prostate gland

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The androgenic steroid hormones testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) have a permissive role in the development of BPH but are not the sole cause. The androgen receptor remains at high levels in the prostate in aging men and specifically in BPH tissues, maintaining responsiveness to androgenic stimuli. The most common of the two 5α- reductase isoforms is type 2 in the benignly enlarged prostate gland. DHT is considered more potent than testosterone by a factor of approximately 10 : 1.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Regarding genetic and familial factors in the etiology of BPH, which statement is TRUE?

options.html: There is no evidence that BPH is a familial disease
Any man who underwent TURP should alert his sons that their chance of having to have TURP is three times greater than age-matched controls
Cases of familial BPH tend to occur in men with smaller prostates than the sporadic cases of BPH
Approximately 50% of cases of BPH in men who undergo surgery when younger than the age of 60 are estimated to be inheritable
The most likely inheritance pattern is autosomal recessive

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There is significant evidence to suggest that some cases of BPH are familial, with autosomal dominant being the most likely inheritance pattern. An increased risk for BPH surgery exists mostly for men who come to BPH surgery when younger than the age of 60, and men with familial cases of BPH have larger glands than men with sporadic cases.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: The prevalence of a disease is defined as the number of:

options.html: diseased people per 100,000 population per year
existing cases per 100,000 population at a distinct target date
cumulative cases of a disease over a specified time period

answer:
The correct answer is B.

When studying diseases by descriptive or analytical epidemiologic methods it is important to have a good understanding of the definitions that apply. Most epidemiologic terms are expressed as rates, which are the number of cases for persons expressed over the population. The definitions that are of relevance are incidence rates = the number of diseased people/100,000 population/year; prevalence = the number of existing cases of the disease of interest/100,000 at a distinct target date; mortality rate, which is the number of deaths/100,000 population/year; and fatality, which equals the number of deaths due to the disease/number of diseased people.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Concerning the autopsy prevalence of BPH or stromoglandular hyperplasia:

options.html: no adequate studies have been done to date
it is commonly found in men of all ages
it is very uncommon in men younger than the age of 30 years
it is found in 100% of men beginning at the age of 40 years
international comparisons are impossible owing to a lack of its definition

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The autopsy prevalence of BPH has been studied as early as 1984 by Berry and colleagues.* Since then, many studies have been done on virtually all continents in many ethnic groups. It is astonishing that these studies find a very significant agreement in terms of the actual prevalence of histologic BPH or stromoglandular hyperplasia around the world. Stromoglandular hyperplasia or BPH is very uncommon in men younger than the age of 30 but then increases steadily in an almost linear manner. In fact, approximately 90% of men in their 80s have evidence of stromoglandular hyperplasia.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is TRUE?

options.html: Moderate symptom severity is defined as a score from 10 to 20 points
The IPSS score addresses irritative and obstructive symptoms and issues of incontinence
Quantitative symptom scores in BPH are not as important as are objective measures such as a flow rate recording
The IPSS score has been translated and validated in many languages
Physicians and nurses may fill out the IPSS score for their patients after consultation

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The IPSS symptom score is a seven-question self-administered questionnaire that yields a total score ranging from 0 to 35 points. Men who score 0 to 7 points are classified as mildly symptomatic, those scoring from 8 to 19 points as moderately symptomatic, and those from 20 to 35 points as severely symptomatic. The IPSS score addresses irritative and obstructive but no incontinence symptomatology. It is widely accepted that quantitative symptom scores are far more important than, for example, urinary flow rate recordings. Fortunately, the IPSS score, the most widely utilized instrument, has been translated and culturally validated in many languages.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which statement is TRUE regarding prostate volume?

options.html: International studies show significant similarity in prostate volume in white, agestratified men.
Prostate volume assessment by digital rectal examination (DRE) is reproducible across examiners
Although there is a steady increase in total prostate volume with age, the transition zone volume increases only marginally
Magnetic resonance imaging measurements are, in general, smaller compared with transrectal ultrasound measurements
DRE estimation of prostate volume is fairly accurate when done by an experienced urologist

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Prostate volume can relatively easily be assessed by transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS). TRUS has been found to be a reliable measure that is reproducible across examiners in contrast to digital rectal examination (DRE), which is only poorly reproducible. MRI is very expensive and it yields in general a larger volume compared with TRUS measurements. Of note is the fact that international studies show significant similarity in regard to total and transitional zone prostate volume in white, age-stratified men.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Concerning liver disease and BPH, which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.html: Ethanol consumption increases circulating levels of estrogens
The risk of having surgery for BPH is increased in heavy drinkers
The intake of ethanol can decrease serum testosterone levels by a variety of mechanisms
Most autopsy studies find a higher prevalence of BPH in men with liver cirrhosis
In men with liver disease histologic specimens of the prostate show a similar influence of estrogen such as seen in hormonally treated prostate cancer

answer:
The correct answer is C.

It is known that alcohol intake may decrease plasma testosterone levels by reducing production of and increasing clearance of testosterone. However, despite this hypothetical reason for a lower incidence, an inverse relationship has been described. The age-adjusted multivariant relative risks for undergoing surgery for BPH in men drinking more than three or four glasses of alcohol per day is lower than in age-matched controls. Of course, this could be due to a bias against surgery in patients who are heavy drinkers and therefore in poor health. It is interesting to note, however, that in the majority of studies, namely, four of five, a lower prevalence of BPH is found in men with cirrhosis compared with those without cirrhosis.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: How do medications influence symptoms and flow rate?

options.html: There is no documented influence of any medication on symptoms or flow rate
Antihistamines and bronchodilators significantly decrease urinary flow rates
Calcium channel blockers and β-adrenergic blockers reduce urinary flow rates significantly
Antidepressants, antihistamines, and bronchodilators increase the symptom score by several points
Anticholinergic agents decrease the peak urinary flow rate markedly

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There is only one study that systematically assessed the effect of medications on urinary symptoms and flow rate. Cold medications containing α-sympathomimetics tend to exacerbate lower urinary tract symptoms by the expected effect on the smooth muscle of the bladder outlet. Data from the Olmsted County Study of Urinary Symptoms and Health Status Among Men show that daily use of antidepressants, antihistamines, or bronchodilators is associated with a 2- to 3-point increase in the symptom score. However, only the daily use of antidepressants is associated with a decrease in the age-adjusted urinary flow rate.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Concerning correlations between baseline parameters, which statement is TRUE?

options.html: A clinically useful correlation exists between prostate volume and serum prostate antigen (PSA) level
Many studies have shown a significant correlation between the transition zone volume and symptom severity
Correlation of symptoms, bother, interference, and quality of life are poor
Urinary flow rate and prostate volume correlate highly with serum PSA level
Serum PSA level shows a strong correlation with symptom frequency and bother

answer:
The correct answer is A.

In general there is an absence of useful baseline correlations between subjective and objective parameters such as symptoms, frequency, quality of life, and urinary flow rate measures of obstruction and prostate volume. However, symptom, bother, and interference with quality of life show excellent correlation with each other, and a clinically useful correlation exists between total and transition zone prostate volume and serum PSA in men with BPH.

stem: What is the most useful first-line test for the diagnosis of prostate cancer?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Combination of DRE and PSA. The DRE and serum PSA are additive and are the most useful first-line tests for assessing the risk that prostate cancer is present in an individual.

stem: Most immunodetectable PSA in sera is bound to which of the following?

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Serum PSA levels vary with which factor?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Age, race, and prostate volume. In the absence of prostate cancer, serum PSA levels vary with age, race, and prostate volume.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Serum PSA elevations are specific for prostate:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

None of the above. Serum PSA elevations may occur as a result of disruption of the normal prostatic architecture that allows PSA to diffuse into the prostatic tissue and gain access to the circulation. This can occur in the setting of prostate disease (benign prostatic hyperplasia [BPH], prostatitis, and prostate cancer) and with prostate manipulation (prostate massage, prostate biopsy). The presence of prostate disease (prostate cancer, BPH, and prostatitis) is the most important factor affecting serum levels of PSA. PSA elevations may indicate the presence of prostate disease, but not all men with prostate disease have elevated PSA levels. Furthermore, PSA elevations are not specific for cancer.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: A 60-year-old man taking finasteride (Proscar) for 2 years with a PSA value of 4 ng/mL would most likely, if he were not taking finasteride, have which PSA value?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

8 ng/mL. Finasteride (a 5α-reductase inhibitor for treatment of BPH) at 5 mg has been shown to lower PSA levels by approximately 50% after 12 months of treatment. Thus one can multiply the PSA level by 2 to obtain the “true” PSA level of a patient who has been taking finasteride for 12 months or more. After 2 and 7 years of finasteride therapy, the PSA level should be multiplied by a factor of 2.3 and 2.5, respectively. Men who are to be treated with finasteride should have a baseline PSA measurement before initiation of treatment and should be followed with serial PSA measurements. If there is a rise in the PSA value when the patient is taking finasteride, these men should be suspected of having an occult prostate cancer.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The knowledge checks inside the week's Elentra asynchronous learning modules, transcribed into the Meds 2025 block bank.
stem: Which of the following statements about prostate cancer staging is FALSE?

options.html: A goal of staging is to predict prognosis
Staging facilitates the selection of rational therapy on the basis of predicted extent of disease
Imaging can accurately identify all cases of pelvic lymph node metastases
PSA and DRE are components of the staging evaluation
Pelvic lymphadenectomy is the gold standard for the detection of pelvic lymph node metastases

The correct answer is C.

Imaging can accurately identify all cases of pelvic lymph node metastases. The goals in staging of prostate cancer are twofold: (1) to predict prognosis and (2) to rationally select therapy on the basis of predicted extent of disease.

All of the above. The currently available modalities for assessing disease extent in men with prostate cancer are DRE, serum tumor markers, histologic grade, radiographic imaging, and pelvic lymphadenectomy.

The correct answer is A.

PSA. Pathologic staging is more useful than clinical staging in the prediction of prognosis because tumor volume, surgical margin status, extent of extracapsular spread, and involvement of seminal vesicles and pelvic lymph nodes can be determined.

stem: A 50 yr old man with known advanced chronic kidney disease from type 2 diabetes presents to the urgent care clinic with worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a peripheral edema. His heart rate is 90 beats/minute and his blood pressure is 150/90. His oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. The rest of the physical exam is normal apart from mild pedal edema. He undergoes arterial blood gas sampling from his radial artery. Which of the following arterial blood gases are most consistent with simple chronic metabolic acidosis due to renal failure: Normal >85 40 24 7.35-7.45 (mmHg) (mmHg) (mmol/L) pO2 pCO2 HCO3 pH
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The pH is low which is compatible with an acidosis. The bircarbonate is low, which is consistent with a metabolic acidosis. The ratio of the change in pCO2 and change in bicarbonate is 1:1 which is compatible with a simple metabolic acidosis

stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding the anatomy of the nephron?

options.html: The lumen of the efferent arteriole is more dilated than the afferent arteriole
The macula densa secretes renin when low blood flow is detected
The efferent arteriole becomes the vasa recta which surround the tubules
The renal medulla receives more blood flow than the renal cortex

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The lumen of the afferent arteriole is more dilated than the efferent arteriole –the efferent arteriole is kept vasoconstricted by angiotensin II, which contributed to increased pressure and filtration in the glomerulus. The macula densa play a role in sensing the ionic (chloride/sodium) content of the urine in the thick ascending portion of the loop of henle. The juxtaglomerular cells that surround the afferent arteriole release renin after detecting changes in afferent blood flow. The renal medulla receives less blood flow than the renal cortex – this makes the renal medulla more sensitive to changes in blood flow.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: The kidneys purify blood by filtering it and reabsorbing nutrients. Beginning in the glomerulus, what is the correct pathway of ultrafiltrate within the nephron? (note: not all substructures are listed)

options.html: Glomerulus -> distal tubule -> proximal tubule -> loop of Henle -> collecting duct
Glomerulus -> proximal tubule -> distal tubule -> loop of Henle -> collecting duct
Glomerulus -> loop of Henle -> distal tubule -> proximal tubule -> collecting duct
Glomerulus -> distal tubule -> loop of Henle -> proximal tubule -> collecting duct
Glomerulus -> loop of Henle -> proximal tubule -> distal tubule -> collecting duct
Glomerulus -> proximal tubule -> loop of Henle -> distal tubule -> collecting duct

answer:
The correct answer is F.

From the glomerulus, filtrate travels through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal tubule and ultimately the collecting duct.

stem: Which of the following changes/hormones would lead to a decreased glomerular filtration rate?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Angiotensin II secretion leads to vasoconstriction of the efferent arteriole which increases the GFR. Prostaglandin secretion leads to afferent arteriole dilation and an increase in GFR. Increasing the HR increases the hydrostatic pressure of the blood and contributes to increase GFR. Noradrenaline constricts the afferent arteriole, decreasing the GFR.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following statements are correct?

options.html: Juxtaglomerular cells can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR
Juxtaglomerular cells can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasodilate to increase GFR
The macula densa can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR
The macula densa can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasodilate to increase GFR

answer:
The correct answer is C.

When the osmolarity of the filtrate is increased, the macula densa (located in the thick ascending loop of Henle) detects this change and signals the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR. This feedback mechanism is called the “Tubulo-Glomerular Feedback”.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which statement below on the RAAS system is true?

options.html: Aldosterone primarily binds to cells within the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Renin reduces blood pressure by ultimately reducing the amount of aldosterone in the blood
Aldosterone secretion leads to reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidney, and vasoconstriction
Granular cells in the afferent arteriole sense ionic strength of the blood and the macula densa secretes renin

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Granular cells secrete renin, which activates the RAAS pathway leading ultimately to increased aldosterone in the blood. Aldosterone predominantly acts on cells in the collecting duct, by increasing the reabsorption of sodium and water. Aldosterone is also a vasoconstrictor.

stem: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is affected by several hormones. Which relationship below is true?

options.html: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and increase the GFR
Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and decreases the GFR
Noradrenaline constricts the afferent arteriole and increases the GFR
Angiotensin II-receptor antagonists dilate the efferent arteriole and increase the GFR

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and increases the GFR. Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) constricts the afferent arteriole and decreases the GFR. Angiotensin II blockade dilates the efferent arteriole and decreases the GFR.

stem: Which of the following regions of the nephron are implicated in excessive calcium excretion in the urine, and what agent can be used to resolve this?

options.html: Thiazides can be used to increase calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubules
Loop Diuretics can be used to increase calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb
Potassium sparing diuretics can be used to increase calcium reabsorption in the collecting ducts
Aldosterone antagonists can be used to increase calcium reabsorption in the collecting ducts

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter at the apical surface which increases passive reabsorption of calcium from the urine. Loop Diuretics contribute to calcium secretion into the urine, by disrupting the Na-K-2Cl transporter. Potassium sparing diuretics block the sodium channels in the collecting ducts which disrupt potassium secretion into urine.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding nephron physiology is correct?

options.html: The distal convoluted tubule is the region where most of the solute is reabsorbed
The descending loop of Henle is permeable to solutes and water
The ascending loop of Henle is permeable to solute but not water
As the filtrate goes deeper into the loop of Henle it becomes more dilute

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The ascending loop of Henle is permeable to solute but not water, while the descending loop of Henle is permeable to water but not solute. As the filtrate passes into the loop of Henle and goes deeper into the medulla down the descending loop, it loses water but retains solute, so it becomes more concentrated (not diluted). The proximal convoluted tubule is where 50-60% of the solute is reabsorbed.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Select the true statement on reabsorption of nutrients by the nephron

options.html: The descending loop of Henle reabsorbs less water than the ascending loop of Henle
Most calcium is reabsorbed by alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Throughout the nephron, intracellular Na+ is kept high and intracellular K+ is kept low by Na/K-ATPase
As more ADH is secreted, urine becomes more concentrated due to increased reabsorption of water in the collecting ducts

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water, whereas the ascending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to sodium. Most calcium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubules. Na/K-ATPase is the driving force of ion gradients in the kidney; however, it keeps intracellular sodium low and intracellular potassium high. Higher ADH secretion stimulates water reabsorption leading to more concentrated urine.

stem: Liddle syndrome is a genetic condition that affects the principal cells of the kidney. In patients with Liddle syndrome, the protein channel that allows for the reabsorption of sodium by principal cells is unable to leave the apical membrane, leading to increased sodium reabsorption. What complication is expected in a patient with Liddle syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Increased sodium reabsorption leads to hypernatremia, and consequently hypertension and increased water retention. However, reabsorption of sodium leads to an increased secretion of potassium, which could lead to hypokalemia.

stem: Which of the following options correctly lists the structures the surgeon would need to dissect to access the kidneys using a posterior surgical approach, from most superficial to most deep?

options.html: Pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, renal capsule
Perirenal fat, peritoneum, pararenal fat, renal capsule
Pararenal fat, renal capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia
Perirenal fat, pararenal fat, peritoneum, renal capsule

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The pararenal fat lies superficial to the renal fascia. The renal fascia encapsulates the kidneys, suprarenal glands and perirenal fat. The renal capsule is the fibrous capsule which sheathes the kidneys.

stem: A patient presents to your office with lateral back pain at the T11 level. After taking a thorough history and performing a physical exam, you suspect this patient may have ureteric stones. Given the region of the radiating pain, which of the following locations would the ureteric stones likely be constricted in?

options.html: Passing into the wall of the bladder

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ureteric pain is characterized by sharp pain in T11-L2 region (loin to groin), and as the stones pass through the ureter the level of pain radiates accordingly given the location in the Ureter. T11 pain is where the kidneys are located, thus ureteric stones would likely be stuck in the renal pelvis as they are entering the ureter. The urethra is distinct from the ureter – the ureter enter the bladder, while the urethra exits the bladder.

stem: Which statement below is a correct difference between the left and right kidneys?

options.html: The arteries supplying the left kidney are shorter than those supplying the right kidney
The left kidney is more inferior than the right kidney
The right renal vein receives deoxygenated blood from the right gonadal vein; the left renal vein does not receive deoxygenated blood from the left gonadal vein
The right renal artery runs anterior to the inferior vena cava, whereas the left renal artery runs posterior to the descending aorta

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The aorta sits on the patient’s left side, and the inferior vena cava sits on the patient’s right side. This means that the left renal artery is shorter than the right renal artery, and that the left renal vein is longer than the right renal vein.

stem: Which location is NOT one of the most common sites for a kidney stone to obstruct the ureter?

options.html: Where the major calyx meets with the minor calyx
At the junction of the renal pelvis and the ureter
Where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim
At the ureteric orifice in the bladder

answer:
The correct answer is A.

There are three natural constrictions in the ureters where kidney stones are likely to obstruct. These are: the junction of the renal pelvis and the ureter, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, and at the ureteric orifice in the bladder.
