stem: Outline the correct order of structures that urine passes through from the collecting duct to the bladder. (note: not all substructures are listed.)

options.html: Collecting duct -> renal pelvis -> major calyx -> ureter -> bladder
Collecting duct -> minor calyx -> renal pelvis -> ureter -> bladder
Collecting duct -> major calyx -> ureter -> renal -> pelvis -> bladder
Collecting duct -> renal column -> renal pelvis -> ureter -> bladder
Collecting duct -> minor calyx -> major calyx -> renal column -> bladder

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Urine leaves the renal pyramid and enters the minor calyx. It is then fed into the major calyx, to the renal pelvis, to the ureter. Finally, the ureter connects to the bladder.

stem: Taylor is a 55-year-old female patient presenting to your clinic in a distressed tachypneic state. A physical exam reveals pitting edema to the level of the kneecap. Which of the following statements is likely correct?

options.html: The patient likely has low serum sodium
The patient likely has high serum sodium
The patient likely has high interstitial levels of sodium
The patient likely has low interstitial levels of sodium.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The pitting edema of the shin reveals ECF overload which is due to elevated total body sodium. Hyponatremia and Hypernatremia indicate water handling issues and suggest that the patient needs to consume less or more water, respectively.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following are valid treatment options for Taylor (from the previous question) to address the cause of her pitting edema?

options.html: Advise the patient to drink more water
Advise the patient to consume more dietary salt
Consider administering an isotonic saline solution

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Taylor’s pitting edema is suggestive of high interstitial levels of sodium. To relieve this, diuretics should be used to free the fluid in the extracellular space (the plasma and interstitium). This can be complicated in situations where the patient may have low plasma volume (hypernatremia). Saline is often given to patients who are volume contracted, to increase the volume of the interstitial region.

stem: Which of the following best illustrates the mechanism by which ADH functions?

options.html: It allows cells of the thick ascending loop of Henle to form aquaporins so water can flow into the filtrate
It increases the activity of transport pumps in the descending loop of Henle so more water can be absorbed
It allows cells of the collecting ducts to form aquaporins so water can flow into the interstitium
It decreases the activity of transport pumps in the distal convoluted tubule so less solute is absorbed

answer:
The correct answer is C.

ADH primarily leads to the formation of aquaporins (water channels) in the collecting ducts so water can flow out of the filtrate into the interstitum. ADH also increases the activity of transporters in the thick ascending limb.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Renal Anatomy, Filtration, Sodium, Water & Acid-Base
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following physiological changes would NOT be expected in a patient who develops hypernatremia?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Patients with hypernatremia have too little water. As a result of being in a hypertonic solution, brain cells lose water by osmosis and shrink. Hyperosmolarity of the blood leads to increased secretion of ADH, leading to increased thirst. With elevated hypernatremia, aldosterone levels (which result in sodium reabsorption in the kidney) would also be reduced to preserve fluid volumes.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Christopher is a marathon runner. During one of his marathons on a hot July day, he was sweating heavily and replenishing with water on road-side tables at every 2-km mark. After the race, he drank another one liter of water. He started feeling confused and weak due to critical hyponatremia. What physiological response was happening in this situation?

options.html: Chris’s brain cells were shrinking due to a hypotonic extracellular fluid
Chris’s adrenal glands were secreting less aldosterone
Chris’s hypothalamus was not secreting ADH

answer:
The correct answer is D.

By consuming too much free water, Christopher’s blood would become hyponatremic. Christopher’s kidneys would compensate by creating dilute urine. For this to happen, he would need to produce less ADH and increase the GFR. Note, consuming free water leads to hyponatremia. Secreting less aldosterone would lead to the loss of even more sodium. Finally, excess water consumption leads to fatal brain swelling (not shrinking)

stem: Which of the following options would suggest a diagnosis of nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus in a patient with hypernatremia and a high urine volume?

options.html: low urine osmolality that responds to exogenous ADH (urine becomes more concentrated)
low urine osmolality that does not respond to exogenous ADH
high urine osmolality with low sodium and potassium concentrations
high urine osmolality with high sodium and potassium concentrations

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Diabetic Insipidus is characterized by high volume urine that is very dilute. A nephrogenic cause is when the kidneys themselves don’t respond to ADH - thus if the kidneys don’t respond to ADH and they have a high volume low osmolarity state that persists the diagnosis of nephrogenic DI should be considered. Central DI is when the production or secretion of ADH is inhibited, and exogenous ADH should lead to a change in urine output.

stem: Manfred is a 34-year-old with undiagnosed Type 2 diabetes. In Type 2 diabetes, the pancreas properly synthesizes insulin; however, cells do not respond to it, leading to elevated serum glucose levels. Manfred is presenting to his family doctor for the first time with symptoms of Type 2 diabetes. Which of the following blood test results or physical examination results are expected?

options.html: Manfred’s urine is high in sodium and potassium.
Manfred has high blood plasma sodium concentrations.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In Type 2 diabetes, the increased sugar in the blood allows for osmotic diuresis in the urine, leading to increased urine production with high urine osmolarity. Therefore, Options A and B are both false. Osmotic diuresis like this leads to urine with low ion concentrations, so Option C is false. The excess free water excretion leads to volume depletion and therefore hypernatremia - Option D is true.

stem: What are two potential causes of cerebral edema?

options.html: Correction of hyponatremia that is too slow
Correction of hyponatremia that is too quick
Correction of hypernatremia that is too slow
Correction of hypernatremia that is too quick

answer:
The correct answer is A, D.

Hyponatremia causes the cells in the brain to absorb more water by osmosis, leading to fatal brain swelling. If this is not corrected quickly enough, this can lead to cerebral edema. On the other hand, in conditions of hypernatremia, the brain adapts by accumulating electrolytes and osmolytes to prevent shrinking. Rapidly correcting the hypernatremia will result in a paradoxical cerebral edema.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Mr. Taylor presents to the ER in a distressed and fatigue state. After the patient's vitals are taken and maintained, an arterial blood gas is taken which reveals the patient has metabolic acidosis. ABG values are displayed below. Which of the following pathologies is the patient likely NOT suffering from? pH: 7.25 HCO3-: 12 Anion gap: 20
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis (drop in bicarbonate levels). The patient also has a large anion gap, which can indicate that other organic acids are accumulating as bicarbonate levels are decreasing. The acronym MUDPILES can be used to find a cause for AGMA: Methanol Poisoning, Uremia, Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Phenformin, Iron Poisoning, Lactic Acidosis, ethylene glycol poisoning, salicylate poisoning. In NAGMA, such as in osmotic diarrhea large amounts of bicarbonate are lost, however chloride ions can be increasingly reabsorbed to make up for the difference.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: In the previous question, Mr. Taylor’s PCO2 was intentionally not given. If he was mounting an appropriate respiratory response to his metabolic acidosis, what should his CO2 levels be?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

If the patient had mounted an appropriate respiratory response by breathing more (to expel more CO2) there would be an equivalent reduction in CO2 as there was in HCO3- (1:1 ratio). Since Bicarbonate decreased by 12, CO2 should have also decreased by 12 (and 40 – 12 = 28).

preamble.title: Shared instructions
preamble.html:
The next three questions correspond to the following scenario.

You are a first-year resident in emergency medicine and your attending physician is quizzing you

on the diagnosis of one of her patients. The 24-year-old patient’s mother found her unconscious

and subsequently called EMS. Since the patient was unconscious, no patient history could be

obtained. A portion of the patient’s bloodwork is shown below.

Blood pH: 7.24

pCO2: 29 mmHg

HCO3-: 14 mmol/L

serum Na+: 136 mmol/L

serum Cl-: 110

albumin: 40 g/L

urine pH: 6.3

stem: What is the patient’s underlying condition?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient’s blood is less than 7.40, signifying acidosis. PCO2 is decreased by 11 mmHg (from the normal value of 40 mmHg), and the patient’s HCO3- is decreased by 10 mmol/L (from the normal value of 24 mmol/L). This is an approximate 1:1 ratio, implying a metabolic cause of the acidosis.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: What is this patient’s anion gap?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The anion gap is calculated by: [Na+] - [Cl- + HCO3-]. Given the patient’s blood results, the anion gap is [136 - (110+14)] = 12. With a normal albumin level of 40 g/L, this anion gap is normal.

stem: Based on the rest of the bloodwork and anion gap, what are some possible causes for this disturbance of the ABG values? Choose the best two answers.

options.html: Loss of bicarbonate from the GI tract
Loss of stomach acid by excess vomiting
Retention of H+ by the distal tubule
Failure of the proximal tubule to reabsorb bicarbonate

answer:
The correct answer is D, E.

This is a case of non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Generally, this can be caused by loss of bicarbonate or retention of protons. The key value in this question is the urine pH of 6.3 (typical urine pH is 5 or less). This signifies that the tubules are not secreting H+, or that the proximal tubules are not reabsorbing HCO3-. If the urine pH was not provided, Option A is another possibility. Excess vomiting would lead to alkalosis, and methanol poisoning would present with an anion gap.

stem: A patient presents to the ER in a state of distress. An ECG displays long slender T waves and a slightly stretched out QRS complex. The patient’s family reports the patient may have been accidentally doubled their dose of Enalapril (an ACE-inhibitor). Which of the following statements is likely correct?

options.html: The patient is hyperkalemic – the Enalapril led to a decreased reabsorption of sodium and increased retention of potassium
The patient is hyperkalemic – the Enalapril led to an increased reabsorption of sodium and decreased retention of potassium
The patient is hypokalemic – the Enalapril led to a decreased reabsorption of sodium and increased secretion of potassium
The patient is hypokalemic – the Enalapril led to an increased reabsorption of sodium and decreased secretion of potassium

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The long slender T waves and stretched out QRS waves are indicative of hyperkalemia leading to cardiac arrhythmia. The ACE-i also indirectly inhibits the secretion of aldosterone. Normally aldosterone leads to sodium retention which consequently draws potassium into the urine (due to the charge gradient).

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A patient presents with hypokalemia. In addition to this they have a high TTKG (11) and on physical exam they have extensive pitting edema up to the level of their kneecap. Which of the following options best explain the patient’s presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Excessive aldosterone secretion leads to increased reabsorption of sodium, which can manifest as pitting edema and fluid build-up throughout the body. Increased reabsorption of sodium in the collecting ducts can promote potassium secretion into the urine (as potassium flows down the charge gradient) – this is in line with the high TTKG which shows increased loss of potassium.

stem: Bill is 67 years old, and his wife brought him to the emergency room after a fall resulting in pain and bruising at his hip. An X-ray revealed a hip fracture. His medications are hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure and insulin for his Type 2 diabetes. Blood tests revealed hyperkalemia (7.0 mmol/L), but his ECG and cardiac functions were completely normal. What is the most likely reason behind his abnormal test results?

options.html: Bill accidentally doubled his insulin dose this morning.
Bill’s blood sample sat around for too long before analysis.
Bill’s thiazide-diuretics inherently lead to hyperkalemia.
Bill has osteoporosis, leading to increased serum calcium and phosphate levels.
Bill’s pain has activated his sympathetic nervous system, leading to an activation of the RAAS pathway.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Elevated potassium levels lead to visible changes in a patient’s ECG. If the ECG is normal, it indicates pseudo-hyperkalemia, in which blood samples sat around for too long before analysis. Taking too much insulin would lead to hypokalemia. Thiazide-diuretics increase the excretion of potassium leading to hypokalemia. Elevated calcium leads to hypercalcemia (not hyperkalemia, although the two look and sound similar!). Increased RAAS activation leads to more sodium reabsorption and more potassium excretion, once again leading to hypokalemia.

stem: Which of the following fluids should be considered for a hypovolemic patient? Select all that apply.
answer: BD. In cases of hypovolemia, fluids administered should stay within the ECF and not into the ICF. Dextrose distributes into the ICF and ECF in a 2:1 ratio. Free water also distributes in a 2:1 ratio to the ICF and the ECF, but the addition of a hypo-osmotic fluid like free water would lead to cell lysis at the point of injection. Normal saline and colloid solutions distribute in the ECF. 482.

stem: A 60-kg patient is scheduled to undergo a 5-hr surgery. During the surgery, how much maintenance fluids should the anesthesiologist deliver to maintain euvolemia?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The maintenance rate rule-of-thumb for IV fluids follows the 4:2:1 rule. For the first 10 kg, a patient receives 4 mL/kg/hr. For the second 10 kg, a patient receives 2 mL/kg/hr. Anything beyond 20 kg, the patient receives an additional 1 mL/kg/hr. For a 60 kg patient, this amounts to (40+20+40) mL, or 100 mL/hr.

stem: Which of the following formulas/markers is ideal for measuring glomerular filtration rate?

options.html: Blood urea nitrogen and Cockcroft-Gault equation
Blood urea nitrogen and CKD-EPI formula

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Serum creatinine levels and the CKD-EPI formula are the best indicators for glomerular filtration rate. Serum Creatinine is a more reliable measure of GFR than BUN because urea can be reabsorbed by the kidney. Serum creatinine is comparatively relatively more stable.

stem: A patient presents with glomerulonephritis. Which of the following findings would you expect to see in their microscopic urinalysis?

options.html: Casts filled with white blood cells
Casts filled with red blood cells

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The presence of casts filled with RBCs can be suggestive of glomerulonephritis. The presence of casts filled with WBCs can be suggestive of Interstitial nephritis. White blood cells can be suggestive of a urinary tract infection and RBCs can be suggestive of cancer or kidney stones.

stem: Which statement of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is true?

options.html: Elevated BUN levels are pathognomonic for a decrease in renal function.
The gold standard for assessing GFR is observing how much insulin is passed by the kidneys
Patients with larger muscular build will inherently have larger creatinine levels than patients with smaller muscular build
GFR tests involving Cystatin C are accurate for adults but do not provide valid results for children

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Creatinine levels are affected by many things, including muscle mass. Elevated BUN levels could indicate many different pathologies. Option B would be true if the answer said inulin, not insulin. Lastly, Cystatin C is a good test for children, but less valid for adults.

stem: Kenneth is 76 years old with a lifelong history of smoking, excess alcohol consumption, and a high cholesterol diet. In recent years, his kidney function has declined considerably. Recently, he has developed painful urination and hematuria consistent with kidney stones. Which imaging modality should be used to confirm the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

An ultrasound is a good first test. CT scans with contrast are valuable tests in general, but with Kenneth’s reduced kidney function, the contrast agent could be too dangerous for him.

stem: A 50-year-old patient with suspected heavy metal ingestion (occupation as a steelworker) undergoes a urinalysis, which reveals moderate protein uremia. The patient’s urine albumin levels are normal however the presence of Tamm Horsfall protein is identified. Which of the following pathologies is the patient most likely to develop, and what is an appropriate management step? Choose two answers.

options.html: Order an ANA and anti-DNA test

answer:
The correct answer is B, G.

The presence of Tamm Horsfall protein (or B2 microglobulin) indicates the patient may have tubular proteinuria. This can result from heavy metal, or any disease that damages the PCT. This is often not associated with any pathological condition – thus no further treatment is required.

stem: A 65-year-old patient with a long history of unmanaged Type 2 Diabetes undergoes a urinalysis, which reveals heavy protein uremia. The patient’s urine albumin levels are high and meet the criteria for proteinuria. Which of the following pathologies is the patient most likely to develop, and what is an appropriate management step? Choose two answers.
answer:
The correct answer is A, F.

The presence of high albumin levels (proteinuria) and the long history of T2D is characteristic of a patient presenting with glomerular proteinuria. Investigations are required for suspicions for glomerular proteinuria- this can involve a CBC count with electrolytes, in addition complement levels, protein electrophoresis, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, ANA, anti-DNA and a Hepatitis B/C serology.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease

stem: Which statement below, pertaining to proteinuria, is correct?

options.html: A patient with transient proteinuria should be referred to a nephrologist.
Multiple myeloma can be screened for with a dipstick urinalysis.
Urinalysis via dipstick is a good screening tool for early kidney disease.
A urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of >20:1 will likely lead to a diagnosis of macroalbuminuria

answer:
The correct answer is D.

A screening test with an albumin-to-creatinine ratio of more than 20:1 is suggestive of macroalbuminuria. This patient would need a 24-hr urine collection to confirm the diagnosis. Option A is false, transient proteinuria is benign. The dipstick urinalysis picks up albumin only, not the light chain that is present in patients with multiple myeloma. Urinalysis via dipstick is cheap and easy, but it is not too sensitive and can miss early kidney disease.

stem: What is the likely pathology when a patient presents with hematuria but no proteinuria?

options.html: This could be a kidney stone in the ureters
This could be natural progression of Type 2 Diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This suggests a structural issue, such as the presence of an obstruction in the ureters like a kidney stone. Glomerular hematuria is characterized by high urine albumin levels (proteinuria).

stem: Which of the following statements regarding chronic kidney disease is true?

options.html: To meet the criteria of CKD, patients need kidney damage and an eGFR below 60 ml/min
The incidence of CKD is decreasing in the overall population
Patients with CKD are contraindicated for ACEi and ARBs
It’s not uncommon for older individuals (older than 80) to have a low (<60 mL/min) GFR

answer:
The correct answer is D.

To meet the criteria of CKD patients need kidney damage OR a reduced eGFR below 60 ml/min. The incidence of CKD is increasing as people are living longer lives. Patients with CKD often require ACEi and ARBs to manage their blood pressure and prevent further decline of their GFR.

stem: After a prolonged period of time not seeing his primary care physician, Todd was diagnosed with Stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Which option below would NOT be a component in his management plan?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

In chronic kidney disease, the treatments are to control blood pressure (eg, reduce salt in the diet), control hyperlipidemia (eg, prescribe a statin), reduce the GFR (eg, with ACE-i’s or ARBs), and restrict protein consumption in the diet. Dialysis is for patients with end-stage renal failure.

stem: You are a resident doctor in the emergency room currently overseeing four patients with renal pathologies. Your attending physician has instructed you to pick one patient to receive dialysis treatment. Whom do you pick for renal dialysis?

options.html: A patient with blood pH of 7.23, PCO2 of 20 mmHg, and [HCO3-] of 20 mmol/L
A patient who has overdosed on salicylates
A patient with Stage 4 chronic kidney disease

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Indications for dialysis are metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalances, ingestion of drugs or ischemia, overload of fluid, or uremia. The patient in option B has respiratory acidosis. Only the patient in option C satisfies any of these indications for dialysis. Patients with Stage 5 Disease (GFR <15%) can be considered for dialysis.

stem: A patient presents with a diaphragmatic hernia, and the diagnostic imaging reveals the abdominal organ is invading the thoracic cavity through the hiatus in the central tendon of the diaphragm. Which of the following structures can be directly impinged by an abdominal organ proceeding through this opening?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The inferior vena cava proceeds into the abdominal cavity via the caval opening located in the central tendon. The abdominal aorta proceeds through the opening made by the left and right crus. The esophageal hiatus is a muscular hiatus where the esophagus passes through. The thoracic duct also proceeds through the aortic hiatus.

stem: An injury to the femoral nerve can lead to a loss of motor innervation to which muscle?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve. The anterior rami innervates the Psoas major and minor, and the Quadratus Lumborum.

stem: What is a possible cause for the abnormality shown on the CT scan below?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

In this CT scan, the patient is missing their right kidney! This is caused by renal agenesis, where the ureteric bud fails to branch off of the metanephros, when there is an absent metanephrogenic blastema, or when the metanephrogenic blastema is not penetrated by the ureteric bud.

stem: Which option below correctly matches an anatomical structure with its embryological origin?

options.html: The kidney develops from the mesonephros
The adrenal glands develop from the pronephros
The ureters develop from the metanephros
The renal arteries develop from the hemanephros

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The mesonephros and pronephros serve functions only in the embryo. The renal system is derived from the metanephros. Hemanephros is a made-up term.

stem: Consider the image below of an abdominal aorta. Which statement is true? [Some labels are not as clear as they could be. For clarity, the authors assert that all labels point to blood vessels that branch off of the abdominal aorta.]

options.html: (I) supplies oxygenated blood to the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and ascending colon
(II) is the artery primarily affected in the condition nicknamed “nutcracker syndrome”
(III) is the left gonadal artery, supplying the testes in males and ovaries in females
(IV) supplies the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum

answer:
The correct answer is D.

(I) is the celiac trunk, which supplies fresh blood to the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. (II) is the renal artery. The left renal vein is affected in renal vein entrapment syndrome, also called Nutcracker syndrome. (III) is the RIGHT gonadal artery, which supplies the testes in biological males and ovaries in biological females. (IV) is the inferior mesenteric artery which supplies the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum.

The caval opening is found in the central tendonous area of the diaphragm
The aorta passes through the diaphragm at spinal level T8
The esophagus passes through the diaphragm posterior to where the aorta passes through the diaphragm

answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

The caval opening is found in the central tendenous area of the diaphragm, at spinal level T8. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at spinal level T10, anterior to where the aorta passes through at spinal level T12.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with decreased breathing. Upon further investigation the physician suspects acute kidney injury. The patient’s ongoing medical challenges include IBS-D (diarrhea-predominant IBS). The blood tests reveal an elevated BUN/creatinine ratio (>80:1), and an ultrasound is negative for hydronephrosis. The urinalysis shows no significant findings. Which of the following classifications of acute kidney injury is most plausible?

options.html: Pre-renal AKI secondary to volume depletion
Pre-renal AKI secondary to systemic vasodilation

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The patient’s elevated BUN/creatinine ratio is suggestive of a pre-renal cause. In addition the lack of significant findings in the urinalysis make intrinsic kidney injury unlikely and the negative findings on the ultrasound make post-renal obstructive causes unlikely. The patient’s history of diarrhea can lead to volume depletion consequently leading to acute kidney injury.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with decreased breathing and vascular markings in their extremities. The patient is relatively healthy asides from minor heart issues which prompted a cardiac angiogram a few days earlier. An ultrasound does not reveal any significant findings. Which of the following causes of acute kidney injury is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

In a cardiac catherization, debris is scraped of the wall, the cholesterol crystals can proceed into circulation and occlude small vessels - leading to vascular marking in the patient’s extremities. These cholesterol crystals can also embolize within nephron structures leading to acute kidney injury. This is a disease of exclusion, and treatment is largely supportive.

stem: A 67-year-old patient with a 50% block in his left anterior descending artery went to the interventional cardiology lab for a stent. In this procedure, a catheter is inserted into the radial artery and fed toward the aortic valve. The catheter is threaded into the coronary arteries with the assistance of contrast agent. Two days after the operation, the patient developed nausea and vomiting, with low urine output and rapid, progressive development of peripheral edema. When examined under the microscope, his urine had brown granular casts. Based on this presentation and his blood tests, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient’s urinalysis and blood tests are consistent with acute tubular necrosis. Additionally, the patient’s medical history is consistent with the diagnosis as well. Acute tubular necrosis can occur iatrogenically, in response to contrast agents used in imaging studies.

stem: Ms. Taylor is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. After five years she developed microalbuminuria based on their albumin to creatinine ratio of 10:1. What is the next best step for this patient’s management?

options.html: The patient will likely be asymptomatic, no extra management needed
The patient should be considered for an ACE-I/ARB
The patient has advanced diabetic nephropathy

answer:
The correct answer is B.

This patient has early-stage diabetic nephropathy as indicated by the microalbuminuria (determined from the albumin to creatinine ratio which correlates well to 24-hour urine collection). No further investigation is required. An ACE-I or ARB should be considered to manage this patient’s condition to prevent proteinuria indicative of advanced diabetic nephropathy.

stem: The management for patients with Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) and Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) with nephropathy are slightly different. Which statement(s) below is true? Select all that apply.

options.html: A patient with T2D is screened for microalbuminuria 5 years after diagnosis; a patient with T1D is screened for microalbuminuria immediately
Patients with T2D are prescribed sodium-glucose-co-transport inhibitors (such as dapagliflozin); patients with T1D are not.
Management for both can include ACE-inhibitors, statins, and tight glycemic control.
All patients with both T2D and T1D are recommended to reduce protein in their diet.

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

Patients diagnosed with T2D are screened for microalbuminuria immediately, whereas patients diagnosed with T1D can be screened 5 years after diagnosis. Reduction of dietary protein is recommended for patients if they are already consuming a large amount of protein. The rest of the answers are true.

weekLabel: Week 15 - Renal Function, AKI & Chronic Kidney Disease
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following medications should not be taken together?

options.html: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and loop diuretics

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Patients taking potassium-sparing diuretics reduce potassium secretion in the urine, leading to hyperkalemia. Patients on this diuretic should not take potassium supplements due to their increased risk of hyperkalemia. Loop Diuretics lead to an increased excretion of calcium, magnesium, and potassium (making the patient at risk for hypokalemia) – calcium and potassium supplements can thus be considered for patients. Patients can be placed on multiple diuretics at the same time – loop diuretics can increase diuresis even when thiazide type diuretics or MRA antagonists are working maximally.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding kidney transplantation is true?

options.html: Deceased-donor kidney transplants have a better prognosis for the recipient than living-donor kidney transplants
Current graft survival rate is slightly over 50%
Prednisone is the mainstay of immunosuppression used to manage kidney transplants
Calcineurin Inhibitors are associated with an increase in skin cancer and can be nephrotoxic

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Living- Donor kidney transplants have a better prognosis than deceased-donor kidney transplants. Current graft survival rates are around 90-95%. Tacrolimus is the main agent used to induced immunosuppression for patients who underwent a kidney transplant.

stem: What is the species of bacteria that is most often implicated in urinary tract infections and what is the most suitable antibiotic treatment for it? Choose TWO answers.
answer:
The correct answer is C, H.

E. coli is the most common bacteria leading to urinary tract infections. This is often empirically treated with nitrofurantoin (or maybe Septa -TMP/SMX), to which E. coli is typically susceptible.

stem: Which statement on the treatment of UTIs is correct?

options.html: Geriatric patients with suspected UTI without symptoms should be treated with broadspectrum antibiotics.
Medical management is avoided in women with asymptomatic bacteriuria unless they are pregnant.
Urine cultures are necessary for all suspected UTI infections.
The most common investigation for a UTI is a genitourinary examination.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Option A is false - geriatric patients are prescribed antibiotics only when there are symptoms of a urinary tract infection. Urine cultures are not usually performed in the management of UTIs, however some indications for culture are if the patient is symptomatic and elderly, if there is recurrent cystitis, or if there is a suspicion for a complicated UTI.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following options is an appropriate management technique for a patient who gets recurrent urinary tract infections (two UTIs within six months)?

options.html: Prescribe nitrofurantoin without performing a urine culture
Encourage the patient to drink more water and request a urine culture
Explore dietary options with the patient
No further management is required other than providing reassurance

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Patients with recurrent UTI should have a urine culture done. This is in contrast to those who have a simple uncomplicated UTI, where prescribing antibiotics without a urine culture is appropriate. The urine culture should be used to guide further management steps which include imaging, referral and prophylaxis. Increasing the patient’s water intake can reduce their risk of recurrence and thus should be considered.

stem: Which of the following patients should generally be treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Patients are generally not treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria, however the exception for treatment is for pregnant women. Treating pregnant women can greatly decrease the risk for pyelonephritis, which can cause adverse outcomes for the mother and newborn.

stem: A male patient has an overactive sympathetic nervous system. What may be a consequence of this?

options.html: The patient’s kidneys will produce more urine
The patient’s penis will more easily become erect
The passage of food through the patient’s large intestine will be slowed
The patient’s afferent arteriole will be dilated

answer:
The correct answer is C.

An overactive sympathetic nervous system will lead to a fight-or-flight response, increasing blood pressure, reducing GFR (options A and D are false), and slowing digestion (Option C is false). Erections are promoted by parasympathetic activity, not sympathetic activity.

stem: Which is a method employed by the human body by which the testes are kept at a cooler temperature for the development of healthy sperm cells? Select all that apply.

options.html: Blood enters the testes via the pampiniform plexus to allow for counter-current heat exchange
The cremaster muscle relaxes to lower the level of the testes
The dartos muscles contract to increase the surface area of the scrotum
The prostate enlarges and shrinks to increase blood flow to the pelvic region

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Options A and C are tempting, however, the Pampiniform plexus is how blood leaves the testicles. The Dartos muscles contract to decrease the surface area of the scrotum, leading to thickening of the skin.

preamble.title: Shared instructions
preamble.html:
Use the following question stem to answer the next TWO questions.

A patient presents to the emergency room concerned about pain in his left flank that developed

over the past 2 days. Ultrasound reveals a mass obstructing the patient’s left ureter and

hydronephrosis of the left kidney. The patient’s right ureter and kidney are normal. Urinalysis

reveals a normal creatinine and BUN levels, and no evidence of a UTI. Assume the mass is

benign.

stem: What is the next step in the patient’s management?

options.html: Refer to a urologist for official diagnosis
Immediate and urgent referral to surgery to fix the obstruction
Insertion of a urethral foley catheter to relieve the obstruction
Insertion of a ureteral stent within six weeks of the onset of symptoms

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Ureteric obstructions should be treated within six weeks of the onset of symptoms. If a UTI develops, the urgency increases, and immediate treatment is required. Since the obstruction is in the ureters, a Foley catheter would not be helpful - a ureteric stent is needed.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Shortly after the ureteric obstruction is relieved, the patient develops lethargy and weakness consistent with hypokalemia. What is the most likely underlying cause of this?

options.html: Medications post-operation include thiazide-diuretics, which lead to hypokalemia.
After the obstruction is relieved, the patient can expel large volumes of urine, leading to hypokalemia.
Irreversible kidney damage has led to excess excretion of potassium.
Normal creatinine and BUN levels indicate pre-renal failure leading to hypokalemia.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Relief of a urinary tract obstruction can lead to post-obstructive diuresis, leading to increased urine production and potassium loss. This can lead to hypokalemia. If the obstruction is relieved within six weeks, kidney damage is not likely.

stem: As a physician you’re currently seeing a patient, Taylor (a 35-year-old female) with severe renal colic and an inability to void for the past 12+ hours. Their BUN/creatinine ratio is significantly elevated, and a renal ultrasound reveals bilateral obstruction of the proximal ureters. Which of the following is the NEXT appropriate management step given the findings?

options.html: Perform a ureteroscopy to remove stones

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The patient is experiencing a urinary tract obstruction likely from a stone occluding the proximal ureter. The most immediate management step involves temporarily relieving the obstruction through a ureteral stent placement. Urethral foley catheter or suprapubic catheter are temporizing measures indicated when the patient is experiencing a bladder outlet obstruction. Once the patient is stabilized, stones can be removed through ESWL, ureteroscopy or percutaneous stone removal. Pharmacotherapy can be a definitive treatment to shrink the prostate and relieve obstructions of the urethra for bladder outlet obstructions.

stem: The patient in the previous question (35-year-old Taylor, female), undergoes an appropriate temporary measure and a few days later undergoes an operation to remove the stones occluding her ureters. The patient is discharged from the hospital. Three days later the patient returns to your clinic to report that they’ve been urinating an excessive amount (several liters every day). Which of the following is an appropriate management step, given the patient’s status?

options.html: Consider prescribing an Angiontensin II/ ARB
Order a CT scan to examine for Hydronephrosis
Give reassurance and encourage adequate fluid intake

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Post Obstructive Diuresis is a common occurrence after urinary tract obstruction. This is largely due to disruption in the kidney’s ability to concentrate the urine and is usually a self- resolving process. The physician should reassure the patient and encourage fluid intake to account for the excessive fluid loss. If necessary, a blood test can be ordered to check for serum electrolyte levels (particularly potassium) and signs of hypovolemia such as postural hypotension.

stem: During a regular DRE, a physician notices that his 56-year-old patient has an enlarged prostate. The patient complains of some frequent urination, weak stream, and incomplete emptying upon voiding. Ultrasound tests indicate that the middle lobe of the prostate is enlarged. The patient has been informed of some of the side effects of surgical therapy and instead has chosen a medical management. Which medicine would you prescribe to the patient to shrink the prostate gland?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

5-alpha reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate. Alpha-blockers relax the muscles of the prostate and bladder, improving urine flow. TURP is an invasive treatment not indicated for this patient (who doesn’t want a surgical therapy).

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A 65-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with concerns of frequent urination, a weak stream and increased straining to urinate. The patient has been experiencing these symptoms for the past month and he feels that it takes a significant toll on his everyday life. A urinalysis and urine culture reveals no significant findings. A digital rectal exam is suggestive of a considerably enlarged prostate. Which of the following is an appropriate management to consider to treat the suspected diagnosis. Choose THREE options.
answer:
The correct answer is C, F, G.

The patient is experiencing LUTS (Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms – frequency, urgency, Nocturia, Weak stream, Intermittency, Straining, Incomplete emptying) which is highly suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia. The negative urinalysis and urine culture rules out blood in the urine (suggestive for bladder cancer) and infection. Treatment is usually guided by the patient’s preferences and since this patient is experiencing noticeable QOL decline, all eligible treatments should be considered. Alpha-blockers will help with relaxing the smooth muscle of the prostatic capsule to improve urination. In addition, 5-alpha reductase therapy is indicated when the prostate is enlarged – this medication will shrink the prostate. Surgical options such as TURP can also be considered to resect portions of the enlarged prostate.

stem: Two years ago, 63-year-old Wallace’s PSA levels were slightly elevated at 7 ng/mL. A prostate biopsy was performed indicating the presence of prostate cancer. This year, Wallace’s PSA levels are 14 ng/mL (with notable prostate enlargement since his last physical examination). Wallace is requesting therapy. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Prostate cancer has a good prognosis even if metastasis has occurred
For many patients, the risks of treating prostate cancer outweigh the benefits
Brachytherapy involves surgically shining high-intensity radio-waves on the affected area
TURP is a common treatment choice for prostate cancer

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Prostate screening in Canada is controversial because even with a positive diagnosis, prostate cancer does not often change life expectancy. Many prostate cancer treatments have side effects that a patient is not willing to risk. A comprehensive discussion should be had with patients outlining the risks and benefits of any medical procedure.

stem: The effectiveness of prostate cancer screening is debated by urologists worldwide. Which statement below is correct?

options.html: Elevated PSA tests are highly specific for prostate cancer
The NNT (number needed to treat) to avoid death by prostate cancer with PSA screening is about 1000
Elevated PSA screening tests leading to a positive diagnosis of prostate cancer require surgical management
PSA screening tests are offered for patients ages 40-79

answer:
The correct answer is B.

For every 1000 patients who undergo a prostate-specific-antigen screening test, 1 person avoids death by prostate cancer [more accurately, 1.28 people in 1000, or an NNT of 732]. Elevated PSA tests are not specific for prostate cancer but could indicate many other benign causes. Positive diagnoses of prostate cancer involve active surveillance (rarely surgery). Finally, PSA screening tests are offered for patients aged 50-69.

stem: Which of the following patients should NOT be considered for a serum PSA screening test?

options.html: A 60-year-old male patient presenting for a routine check-up
A 75-year-old male patient presenting for a routine check-up
A 55-year-old male patient who recently had surgical resection of their prostate due to prostate cancer
A 50-year-old male patient who received a digital rectal exam with a reported palpable nodule

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Serum PSA screening should not be offered to males over the age of 70 – their risk of prostate cancer developing to become a limiting illness is very low. Serum PSA should generally be considered for patients above 50 years old and this can involve a discussion between the doctor and patient. Serum PSA is also used post-operatively to determine any possible recurrence of prostate cancer. A palpable nodule on the DRE exam for a male patient (>50 years) should evoke consideration for a serum PSA test.

stem: Which of the following treatments is generally NOT appropriate for early stage prostate cancer?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Radical prostatectomy, brachytherapy and external beam radiation are generally appropriate for patients with early stage prostate cancer. Radical Prostatectomy can also be considered for late stage prostate cancer. Chemotherapy is generally not a part of the treatment for early stage prostate cancer but can be considered for hormone refractory disease.

stem: Billy-Ray was getting an abdominal ultrasound to assess for kidney stones when his physician incidentally found a fluid-filled cyst on Billy-Ray’s right kidney. What is the next step in Billy-Ray’s management in dealing with the cyst?

options.html: Consider obtaining creatinine and BUN levels with a urinalysis
Refer to radiology for a CT scan of the mass
Perform a biopsy to assess staging
No further tests or management is needed

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Fluid filled cysts are very common and benign. No further tests are needed.

stem: What is the goal for management of advanced kidney cancers?

options.html: To improve the patient’s quality of life
To regress the tumour to a more manageable size

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Advanced kidney cancers typically are not curable. Treatment is palliative, aiming to improve the quality of life for patients.

stem: Key feature question, Select the best 3 answers. Which tests is a physician likely to order for a 56-year-old patient if an ultrasound reveals a 3-cm mass on a left kidney and a follow-up CT suggests that the mass is neoplastic?
answer:
The correct answer is D, E, G.

These tests are to stage the cancer (CT of the abdomen and pelvis) and rule out metastasis of the kidney cancer, which occurs most often in the lungs (Chest X-ray / CT of the chest), liver (liver enzymes), lymph nodes (CT of abdomen and pelvis), bone (not listed, but serum ALP levels), and brain.

stem: A 50-year-old male patient undergoes an initial abdominal ultrasound which reveals a unilateral renal mass. Further follow-up with a CT scan shows a large (12 cm) solid enhancing tumor extending from the body of the kidney and involving the renal vasculature. The patient is asymptomatic. Further X-rays reveal no metastasis. Which of the following treatment options is mostly appropriate for this current patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

A radical nephrectomy is most appropriate as this renal tumour is large and involves the surrounding vasculature. Partial nephrectomy or ablation methods are not appropriate for larger tumours with vascular involvement. Palliative radiation is generally reserved for advanced kidney cancer, also this patient is asymptomatic currently.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following characteristics of a renal mass on an investigative test (imaging or biopsy) would generally prompt for further investigation/treatment? Choose as many as applicable.

options.html: A renal mass with internal strictures on ultrasound
Dromendary humps noted on renal ultrasound
A renal biopsy confirming papillary renal cell carcinoma Type 2
A renal mass delineated with a round, smooth, regular borders on ultrasound
A renal mass with enhancement in the corticomedullary phase of the CT scan

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, E.

A renal mass with internal structures is indicative of a complex cyst which can be malignant (low potential). Dromendary humps are not pathological, they are a variation of normal renal anatomy. Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma Type 2 is an aggressive type of cancer in contrast with Type 1 which is more indolent. A renal mass with regular borders and a round/smooth appearance on ultrasound is likely a simple cyst and does not require any follow-up. A renal mass with enhancement in the second phase of a 3-part CT scan, is suggestive of a solid enhancing renal mass which can be malignant and requires follow-up. In general, any renal mass that is not a simple cyst or a dromendary hump should be evaluated by a urologist.

stem: A patient with cancer affecting his left ureter wants a surgical removal of the tumour. How will the surgeon proceed?

options.html: The surgeon will remove the ureter and the kidney even if the kidney is not affected
The surgery will remove the ureter and the kidney only if the kidney is also affected
The surgeon will neither remove the ureter nor the kidney
The surgeon will remove both ureters and both kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Due to the field effect, both the kidney and ureter are removed, even if the kidney is not affected.

stem: What item is not on your differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hematuria?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

BPH, UTIs, Kidney stones, and lower urinary tract tumours can all present with hematuria, and this is an indication to refer to a urologist for further testing. Testicular torsion is acute and presents with a painful swelling of the testicle. This affects the reproductive system and not the urinary system.

stem: A 55-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with concerns of peeing out blood. The patient has worked at a plastic manufacturing plant for the past 20+ years. In addition to hematuria the patient also reports peeing out “stringy clots”. The patient reports no pain when urinating. Which of the following statements is most likely true?

options.html: The patient’s presentation is in line with an upper urinary tract tumour and this may likely require surgical removal of the ureter and kidney
The patient’s presentation is in line with an upper urinary tract tumour and this may likely require surgical removal of solely the ureter
The patient’s presentation is in line with a lower urinary tract tumour and this may likely require surgical removal of the urethra and bladder
The patient’s presentation is in line with a lower urinary tract tumour and this may likely require surgical removal of solely the bladder

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The presence of stringy clots in the urine suggest the source of bleeding comes from the ureter – and when considering the patient’s extensive work history in a plastics history this can make an upper urinary tract tumour a likely diagnosis. Upper urinary tract pathologies involve the kidneys and/or ureter while lower urinary tract pathologies involve the bladder and/or urethra. Due to the field effect (where entire fields of the urothelium are at oncogenic risk) surgical removal of the entire kidney and ureter is often done unless more conservative treatment is required (to preserve kidney function).

stem: A 60-year-old asymptomatic male patient was recently investigated for microscopic hematuria after taking a urinalysis for an unrelated reason. Investigations revealed this patient had a mild, low grade, superficial urothelial bladder cancer. This finding did not require treatment but the patient had to be screened periodically to check for the progression of this disease. Which of the following investigations is most likely used to assess this?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Periodic monitoring is done via cystoscopy – an invasive procedure where the physician can examine the lining of your bladder.

stem: Which imaging modality is most commonly used when a patient presents with a scrotal mass?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

With any scrotal mass, an ultrasound is usually indicated. In many cases, a scrotal ultrasound can lead to the diagnosis of the mass. Transillumination is valuable if suspicious for hydrocele, but not too valuable otherwise. The other imaging modalities become more important to confirm more sinister diagnoses; however, ultrasound is usually the first imaging test ordered.

stem: Which of the following statements is true concerning testicular cancer?

options.html: 10% of all presentations of testicular cancer already involve metastasis
Testicular cancer is very curable if metastasis has not occurred, but not curable otherwise
Testicular cancer can lead to varicocele or hydrocele
Testicular cancer can be staged with an ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The initial presentation of testicular cancer involves metastasis in 10-15% of cases. Common sites of metastasis include the abdomen, the chest, the liver, and the brain.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the ER with severe scrotal pain that began one hour ago. The physician performs a localized physical exam of the testes and notices it’s very firm upon palpation. The physician orders an ultrasound which confirms the physician’s suspected diagnosis. Which of the following is likely true regarding this case?

options.html: The suspected diagnosis was testicular torsion and was confirmed by the presence of arterial blood flow to the affected testicle
The suspected diagnosis was testicular torsion and was confirmed by a lack of arterial blood flow to the affected testicle
The suspected diagnosis was epididymitis and was confirmed by the presence of arterial blood flow to the affected testicle
The suspected diagnosis was epididymitis and was confirmed by the absence of arterial blood flow to the affected testicle

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Testicular torsion often occurs in young males (adolescents) and is accompanied by a sudden onset of pain. The affected testicle are often hard when palpating. Patients with epididymitis are generally older, have a gradual onset of pain, and the testes may tender when palpating. To confidently distinguish the two, an ultrasound can be done – if there is a lack of arterial blood flow this is indicative of testicular torsion, as the twisting cuts off blood supply to the testes. In epididymis there is normal or increased blood flow to the testes.

stem: A 65-year-old patient presented to his family physician after he noticed his scrotum is enlarged. A physical exam is conducted, where the physician asks the patient to stand up – there was no enlargement of veins observed (unilaterally or bilaterally). On palpation the physician noted the scrotum was tense but was able to palpate the two testicles. The physician was also able to “get above the mass” (they could feel the mass tapering, and the scrotum was illuminated on transillumination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Hydrocele is when there is fluid build-up inside the scrotum, which often fives it a tense appearance. To conclusively differentiate a hydrocele from a hernia, a hydrocele can be felt tapering off, whereas the hernia cannot be. Alternatively, the patient can also be asked to cough and see reflective movement in the scrotum or bowel sounds may be heard within the scrotum to identify a hernia. A varicocele is indicated by enlarged veins typically occurring on the left side – not seen in this presentation. Spermatocele occurs from a seminal fluid leak and can often feel like a third testicle is present.

review.t: Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses

stem: Juan is 12 years old and has a blood pressure that is 127/83 mmHg. For his age and height, a 95th percentile for blood pressure is 123/81 mmHg. Maria is 11 years old and has a blood pressure that is 131/85 mmHg. For her age and height, a 95th percentile for blood pressure is 119/78 mmHg. Both Juan and Maria are asymptomatic and secondary etiologies of hypertension have been ruled out. Select ALL the correct statements.

options.html: Juan has Stage 1 hypertension and Maria has Stage 2 hypertension.
Both Juan and Maria should be assessed for white coat hypertension with ambulatory BP monitoring.
Maria requires rapid correction of her blood pressure to the 90th percentile with oral or IV medications.
Juan should be prescribed a CCB, an ACE-I, and diuretics immediately.
Both Juan and Maria require IV medications.

answer:
The correct answer is A, C.

According to 2017 guidelines, Stage 1 hypertension is defined as >95th percentile, and stage 2 hypertension is defined as 95th percentile + 12 mmHg. The treatment for Stage 1 hypertension is to rule out white coat hypertension with an ambulatory BP monitor, rule out secondary etiologies, and then lifestyle management for six months before prescribing medications. The treatment for Stage 2 hypertension is to assess urgency (asymptomatic in the question stem), and then to rapidly reduce BP to the 90th percentile with either oral or IV medications. If Maria was symptomatic requiring emergent treatment, IV medications would be prescribed.

stem: Question 545. Erica is an 8-year-old patient who was brought into a pediatric urgent care clinic. In the past 24 hours, Erica has developed acute shortness of breath, fatigue, and confusion. Upon examination, Erica appears unwell, with elevated BP, pitting edema, and minimal urine output. Blood tests indicate elevated urea and creatinine in the blood consistent with acute kidney injury (AKI). Urinalysis indicates low urine osmolarity and high urine sodium and no evidence of E. coli infection. What is the most likely diagnosis and best treatment option for Erica? Choose TWO answers.
answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

The large volume status, low urine osmolarity, and high urine sodium indicate a renal cause of acute kidney injury. The management for this would be fluid restriction. Dialysis is referred for refractory symptoms (symptoms that aren’t relieved despite best management efforts).

stem: Isaiah is a 5-year-old child with symptoms indicating an acute kidney injury. There is swelling in his legs bilaterally. Urine tests indicate severe proteinuria, low serum albumin, and high serum cholesterol. What is the next best step in Isaiah’s management?

options.html: Perform an ultrasound of Isaiah’s kidneys
Perform a biopsy of Isaiah’s kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Massive proteinuria indicates a nephrotic syndrome. The most common nephrotic syndrome is minimal change syndrome, followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. The treatment for both of these is prednisone (a steroid). Biopsy is indicated if Isaiah was less than 1 years old, if Isaiah had hypertension and hematuria, symptoms of chronic kidney disease, or low C3 levels.

stem: Jeremy is a 6-year-old child with symptoms indicating an acute kidney injury. Yesterday, Jeremy had repeated trips to the bathroom, and today he is edematous. Urine tests indicate hematuria and mild proteinuria. Serum C3 levels were measured and were found to be low. Despite his presentation, there is no evidence of chronic kidney disease. Which statement below is TRUE?

options.html: Jeremy should be referred for a kidney biopsy to rule out C3 glomerulopathy
Jeremy should be started on steroids and immunosuppressants
Jeremy should receive supportive treatment and have C3 levels reassessed in 6 weeks
Jeremy should toughen up and learn to deal with the pain while he is young
Jeremy should receive treatment to boost IgA levels

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Hematuria with mild proteinuria indicates nephritic syndrome. In cases of nephritic syndrome, complement C3 levels are measured. If normal, it indicates IgA nephropathy. If low, it could indicate post-strep glomerulonephritis or C3 glomerulopathy. To assess between these two, a repeat complement C3 level is measured six weeks later. With no symptoms of CKD, steroids and immunosuppressants are not indicated. If, however, C3 levels were low after 6 six weeks, a kidney biopsy is indicated.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is diagnosed with Stage 2 Hypertension after an ambulatory blood pressure was measured to be 145/95 mmHg. The patient presents asymptomatically. Which of the following is an appropriate NEXT step?

options.html: Repeat blood pressure measurements 1 week later to account for
Consider pharmacological treatment with oral Minoxidil
Consider non-pharmacological management (diet modification, exercise, salt restriction)
Perform investigation to rule-out underlying cause for hypertension

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient’s diagnosis of hypertension is accurate as ABP is used and is the goldstandard; white-coat hypertension does not apply to ABP monitoring. This patient presents with asymptomatic stage 2 hypertension which can be classified as hypertensive urgency – the next immediate management step is to rapidly correct BP (down to <90%) to prevent hypertensive emergency using oral/IV medications. Afterwards an investigation for the underlying cause of hypertension is appropriate. Non-pharmacological intervention is not appropriate in isolation for stage 2 hypertension – but this is the first line of therapy for pediatric patients with stage 1 hypertension.

stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding nephrotic syndrome and nephritic syndrome?

options.html: Both nephrotic and nephritic syndrome are characterized by elevated serum urea and creatinine
In nephrotic syndrome oliguria precedes edema
Nephritic syndrome is characterized by renal inflammation
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by mild/normal proteinuria

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Nephritic syndrome is characterized by renal inflammation and nephrotic syndrome is characterized by significant proteinuria. In nephrotic syndrome edema is the starting event and it precipitates oliguria (decreased urine output). Nephrotic syndrome is usually characterized by normal serum urea and creatinine levels while nephritic syndrome is characterized by normal or mildly elevated urea and creatinine levels.

stem: Which of the following findings for a patient being investigated for hemolytic uremic syndrome is suggestive for this disease over a pre-renal injury or renal injury?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Acute Kidney Injury broadly can be characterized by oliguria. Hypovolemia, high urine osmolality and low urinary sodium are suggestive of a pre-renal cause for AKI. Fluid congestion can be suggestive of an intrinsic renal cause. Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome is caused by E. coli induced diarrhea and can manifest as thrombotic microangiopathy – thrombocytopenia and fragmented RBCs.

stem: What is an indication for an ultrasound when a 12-month-old male presents with undescended testis (UDT)?

options.html: Perform an ultrasound if the UTD is unilateral and the testis is palpable
Perform an ultrasound if the UTD is unilateral and the testes is not palpable
Perform an ultrasound if the UTD is bilateral the testes are palpable
Perform an ultrasound if the UTD is bilateral the testes are not palpable

answer:
The correct answer is D.

An ultrasound for undescended testicles is rarely useful. However, it is important to perform an ultrasound in cases of bilateral non-palpable testes to assess if the phenotypically male patient is a chromosomally female patient with congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

stem: Which statement below is correct concerning acute scrotal pain in the pediatric population?

options.html: A patient with testicular torsion should undergo manual detorsion as a first line of therapy.
Doppler ultrasound shows increased blood flow to the ipsilateral testicle in cases of epididymitis.
A Blue-dot sign is observed in most cases of appendage torsion.
Episodes of testicular torsion must be treated within 6 hours to guarantee that an orchidectomy will not be required.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

In cases of testicular torsion, the patient should be referred to an emergency urologist immediately. The “Golden hours” in testicular torsion is 0-6 hours, during which the risk of losing the testicle is somewhere around 5-12% (but not zero). A blue-dot sign can indicate an appendage torsion, but the absence of a blue-dot sign does not rule out appendage torsion as a diagnosis. In epididymitis, blood flow increases to the enlarged testicle; in testicular torsion, blood flow decreases to the enlarged testicle.

stem: You are seeing a 5-year-old female, Ivy, who has exclusive nighttime enuresis, but voids frequently (12 times) during the day. Her void diary was completed, indicating a functional bladder capacity of 150 mL. When you talk to her, she seems embarrassed and ashamed about her bedwetting, but otherwise seems happy and content. She is doing well in school. Which treatment below would NOT be helpful for Ivy?

options.html: Recommend that Ivy and her parents set alarms during the night to establish a nighttime routine
Reassure Ivy and her parents that most cases of nighttime bedwetting self-resolve with time
Suggest consuming less fluids close to bedtime
Prescribe oxybutynin, an anti-cholinergic drug to help manage her symptoms
Ascertain the cause with an MRI of the bladder

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Ivy’s functional bladder capacity is low (normal bladder capacity = (age+2)*30), which can result in nighttime enuresis. Ivy and her parents should be reassured that this will likely self- resolve. MRIs are indicated only if there is a high suspicion for neurogenic issue.

stem: Verne is 4 years old. His mother brought him into the emergency room because of Verne peeing blood. He also has a fever and left flank pain. Urinalysis tests positive for Enterococci. Verne’s mother indicates that this is Verne’s first UTI. As the on-call resident in the emergency department, you are suspicious for vesicoureteral reflux. Given Verne’s presentation, what test do you order?

options.html: Check the creatinine and serum levels to assess for kidney damage
Refer to urology for a voiding cystourethrogram
Refer to urology for a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan

answer:
The correct answer is C.

When vesicoureteral reflux presents with febrile UTIs, a voiding cystourethrogram is indicated to assess for bladder outlines, to grade the VUR, to assess for issues with the urethra, and to assess post-void residual volume. In the case of recurrent febrile UTIs, a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan is used to assess for scarring.

stem: A 8-month-old male is brought into a urologist’s office because his parents are concerned about his testicles. The urologist examines the patient’s scrotum and palpates only one testicle. The urologist can palpate the undescended testicle and bring it down into the scrotum using a physical maneuver, however the testes do not remain there and return to the inguinal region. Which of the following options is an appropriate management step?

options.html: Instruct the family to bring the patient back at 12 months of age, as the testes can spontaneously descend from 6-12 months of age.
The patient has retractile testis – no immediate action needed besides active surveillance
Consider further investigation with an ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This patient has undescended testis. If the patient had retractile testis upon a physical maneuver the patient’s testicle would remain in the scrotum without returning to its original place. Patients who are between 3-6 months do not need to be referred as undescended testis often spontaneously descend. An ultrasound is not specific or sensitive enough to be used in this situation. Since the undescended testicle was palpable in the inguinal region an exploratory laparoscopic examination is not necessary and an inguinal orchidopexy should be considered to surgically place the testicle back in the scrotum.

stem: Which of the following is a distinguishing marker between physiological and pathological phimosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Scarring of the foreskin particularly around the opening is suggestive of pathological phimosis. Steroid treatment and manual retractions are not possible at this point and this requires circumcision. Redness of the foreskin can indicate balanitis and frequent reoccurrence of balanitis can lead to scarring and pathological phimosis.

stem: A 35-year-old patient comes to your clinic with concerns of incontinence. She describes that she often experiences involuntary voiding at work when lifting heavy objects or laughing at someone’s joke. On physical exam no abnormalities are seen, and the patient does not have any prior surgical history. Neurological assessment is normal. Which of the following are appropriate treatments to consider for the presumed diagnosis? Select TWO Answers.
answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

Stress incontinence is when there is urine leakage with increased abdominal pressure (lifting objects, laughing, sneezing, etc.). Urge incontinence is when there is a loss of urine with the urge to void. Pelvic floor exercises and a midurethral sling (surgical) are both appropriate treatments to consider for patients with stress incontinence. Alpha blockers and 5-a reductase are prescribed for male patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia to relax smooth muscles and shrink the prostate. Botox administration and anticholinergic medication is appropriate for urge incontinence.

stem: A 35-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with voiding difficulties. He reports a weak stream, at times intermittent, and he often must strain to urinate. A physical exam of his genitals and abdomen is performed and no abnormalities are present. No significant findings are present on the neurological or surgical history. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate in distinguishing an outlet dysfunction versus a detrusor dysfunction within this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Urodynamics. It can be difficult to distinguish between a detrusor dysfunction (is the bladder weak) or an outlet dysfunction (outlet obstruction) as both will present with the same symptoms. Urodynamics can be used to assess the strength of the bladder contractility and can be used to distinguish between these two dysfunctions. An uroflow examines the flow of urine when voiding. A cystoscopy can be used to examine the lining of the bladder.

stem: You are a family physician seeing Chris, a 68-year-old patient, who has recently been concerned about his urine voiding dysfunction. “I just can’t hold it Doc, 10 or so times a day I get the feeling where I have to go, and once I get the feeling, I need to go BAD.” Based on this presentation, which medication would be best to address Chris’s voiding dysfunction?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Chris’s presentation sounds like an urgency incontinence, and medical management for urgency incontinence is a beta-3 agonist (such as mirabegron). [Another surgical management available for Chris is intravesical Botox injections.] 5-alpha reductase inhibitors shrink prostates, alpha-blockers increase ease of urination, and diuretics increase urine production - all medications that would exacerbate Chris’s presentation of urgency incontinence.

stem: A 34-year-old male patient arrives at the ER in severe pain in his flank region radiating down to the groin. The patient is passing blood with his urine. The patient also has a fever (38.5 degrees). The physician orders a CT KUB and confirms the presence of urinary stones lodged in the ureter. Which of the following is an appropriate management step?

options.html: Consider providing analgesia and give reassurance (most stones pass by themselves)
Administer tamsulosin (an alpha-blocker) to the patient
Perform a percutaneous nephrostomy to drain the kidney
Perform a percutaneous nephrostomy to drain the kidney and then administer antibiotics

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The patient’s presentation must be emergently handled due to their severe pain and existing fever. Their fever places them at high risk for sepsis. To address this the urinary tract must be drained and IV antibiotic therapy must be considered. An alpha blocker can be considered in more conservative situations, in addition to encouraging fluid intake and administering analgesia.

stem: Which of the following management options is NOT appropriate for a patient with urinary stones composed of calcium oxalate?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Calcium stones can either be calcium-phosphate stones or calcium-oxalate stones (more common). To reduce the occurrence of calcium stones, calcium intake should surprisingly be increased – the dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut to prevent oxalate from being absorbed. High water intake and low sodium intake should also be recommended. Increasing Oxalate intake (through eating dark leafy vegetables, teas, strawberries, rhubarb) can increase the occurrence of calcium oxalate stones.

stem: A physician recommends to a patient with urinary stones to increase the potassium citrate in his diet as blood pH alkalization is a key component of management and preventing further urinary stones. Which of the following urinary stones does this patient most likely have?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

This patient could have had uric acid stones or cystine stones, as both of these are treated with alkalinization of the urine. However, between these two, uric acid stones are more common (15%) than cystine stones (<1%)

stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding urinary stones?

options.html: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones typically precipitate in an acidic pH
Shockwave lithotripsy is an invasive procedure to remove stones
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is often indicated for large urinary stones including staghorn calculi
Ureteroscopy is typically used to address stones in the renal pelvis and proximal ureter

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Struvite stones typically precipitate in a basic pH (phosphate precipitates in high pH and this often precipitated by urease producing organisms secreting ammonia in the urine). Shockwave lithotripsy uses shock waves to break up stones and is a non-invasive procedure. Ureteroscopy is typically used to address stones in the mid to distal ureter.

stem: You are a physician working a night shift in the emergency room when Robert comes in with severe left abdominal pain. Your suspicions of a kidney stone are confirmed with an ultrasound. You are waiting for some blood test results to determine the next course of treatment. Which test result is LEAST likely?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Citrate is protective - it binds calcium preventing supersaturation of calcium, and it binds calcium oxalate crystals preventing crystal growth. If Robert had a kidney stone, he could have all of the remaining four options, and possibly hypocitremia.

stem: Which of the following patients would be considered for a combined kidney pancreas transplant?

options.html: A patient with kidney failure and Type 1 Diabetes
A patient with kidney failure and Type 2 Diabetes
A patient with kidney failure who is not yet on dialysis
A patient with kidney failure who has been on dialysis for several years

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A combined kidney and pancreas transplant is a unique transplant where the patient with a failing kidney and Type 1 Diabetes gets both a pancreas and kidney. Type 1 Diabetes can contribute to failing kidney function – the addition of a pancreas transplant can address this contributing cause of kidney decline.
