stem: Which of the following statements about hemodialysis (HD) and/or peritoneal dialysis (PD) is true?

options.html: PD uses negative pressure to filter the blood
Cardiovascular disease is a common complication of PD and HD
HD is associated with better survival than PD
PD is primarily done in hospital settings
Patients receiving HD generally have a better quality of life than those receiving PD

answer:
The correct answer is B.

PD uses an osmotic gradient established by the peritoneum to filter blood, while hemodialysis uses negative pressure. Cardiovascular disease is a common complication of PD and HD and most patients with renal diseases often end up dying from cardiovascular reasons rather than renal causes. PD survival is comparable (or may be better) than HD with regards to patient survival. PD is primarily done in the home, HD is primarily done in hospital settings but can also be set up at home (with patient education). Because of this, HD involves less flexibility and patients have reduced autonomy (and reduced QoL).

weekLabel: Week 17 - Incontinence, Stones & Renal Replacement

stem: Which statement of kidney transplantation is true?

options.html: Hemodialysis is preferred to kidney transplantation in most cases
Transplantation requires immunosuppressants such as tacrolimus
Type 2 diabetics qualify for a combined kidney/pancreas transplant
Cadaveric donors are preferred over live donors

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Tacrolimus is a powerful immunosuppressant used in kidney transplantation. Kidney transplantation, compared with hemodialysis, is associated with better qualities of life and better 10-year survival. Live donors are preferred, but due to donor shortages, most transplants come from cadavers. Note, combined kidney/pancreas transplants are available for patients with Type 1 diabetics, whose pancreases do not produce insulin.

stem: Robert has a kidney stone. Urinalysis results returned, indicating that it is made of calcium oxalate. Which of the following should be recommended to Robert for the management of his kidney stones? Select all that apply.

options.html: Robert should drink more red wine
Robert should consume less oxalic acid in his diet
Robert should increase his salt intake

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, E.

Calcium binds to oxalic acid in the digestive tract, prevent absorption. This increased dietary calcium would benefit patients with calcium oxalate kidney stones. Oxalic acid should be avoided if possible. Finally, increasing fluid-intake is always helpful in the case of kidney stones. [Author’s note: Robert should drink more wine if he was a first-year medical student and just finished his final exam for year 1, assuming he does so responsibly. However, this would not help Robert with his kidney stones.]

options.html: Generalized edema most often reflects cardiac, liver, or renal disease

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, D.

Edema usually presents with volume overload, which can be caused by cardiac, liver, or renal causes. Edema can also present as ascites in the abdomen.

stem: Which of the following is true with respect to Anti-diuretic hormone is true? Choose all that apply.

options.html: It is released from the hypothalamus
It is released in response to ECF volume contraction
Increasing osmolality should shut down ADH production

answer:
The correct answer is A, C.

ADH is released from the posterior pituitary when osmolality is increasing, sensed by the hypothalamus. When osmolality begins to decline, ADH production is shut down.

stem: What is true with respect to diabetes insipidus?

options.html: It can be caused by trauma and infections
It may result from the inadequate production of ADH
It presents with passing large amounts of dilute, tasteless urine

answer:
The correct answer is D.

All the above are true. Diabetes insipidus is associated with increased thirst and drinking and may result from inadequate central production of ADH or inadequate renal response to ADH. It can be caused by injuries or trauma, most often brain injuries and post-op neurosurgery patients.

If symptomatic, treatment with fluids should be fast
The underlying cause should be found and corrected
Access to free water should NOT be restricted

answer:
The correct answer is A, C.

stem:
Which of the following regarding diuretics is correct:

  1. NSAIDs should be avoided/prescribed with caution to patients already taking furosemide, amiloride, or chlorthalidone
  2. spironolactone causes hyperkalemia and hypercalcemia
  3. loops diuretics can be used to treat recurrent calcium kidney stones
  4. triamterene is commonly used as a monotherapy to treat congestive heart failure A. i, ii B. i C. i, iii D. iii, iv E. None of the above
answer: i is the only correct option. NSAIDs should be avoided with these diuretics because NSAIDs impairs potassium and sodium excretion, which decreases the effect of loops diuretics and thiazide (furosemide, chlorthalidone), while also worsening hyperkalemia with K sparing diuretics (amiloride). Spironolactone causes hyperkalemia but not hypercalcemia. Thiazides, not loop diuretics, can be used to treat calcium kidney stones because they increase calcium reabsorption. Triamterene is a K sparing diuretic, so its commonly used in combination with other diuretics to prevent potassium wasting.

stem: A patient with type II diabetes and renal insufficiency is experiencing edema. They are also currently on an ACEi. Which of the following diuretics would be appropriate for them?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Furosemide is a loop diuretic that also increases renal blood flow, which can help with renal insufficiency in this case. Spironolactone and amiloride are K sparing diuretics and aldosterone antagonists, respectively, which could worsen hyperkalemia when used with ACEi. Chlorthalidone is a thiazide and can worsen insulin resistance, so it is not the best option for patients with type II diabetes.

stem: A patient had undergone a kidney transplant and experienced a gradual decline in his renal function over 10 years. His creatinine has been steadily rising and the biopsy showed marked interstitial fibrosis. What is appropriate management for this patient i. Pulse with high dose steroids and gradually taper down to maintenance dose ii. Control underlying hypertension and hypercholesterolemia (if present) iii. Switch CNI to sirolimus iv. Initiate thymoglobulin
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Underlying HTN, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia worsens interstitial fibrosis, thus it’s important to manage in chronic transplant rejection. CNIs are nephrotoxic and induce fibrosis, so switching to sirolimus (weaker) would decrease scarring. Steroid pulse are used to treat acute rejections, not chronic rejections. Thymoglobulin is only indicated in treating severe acute rejections or patients at very high risks of rejection.

options.html: Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with sympathetics to lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes
Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with sympathetics to sacral spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes
Somatic sensory afferents travel directly from the cervix to the spinal cord, and pain is perceived exactly where it is felt
Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with parasympathetics to lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes
Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with parasympathetics to sacral spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The cervix falls below the pelvic pain line. Visceral sensory afferents from structures below the pelvic pain line are unique in that they travel retrograde with parasympathetics to the sacral spinal cord. When the painful stimulus reaches the brain, it is perceived as coming from sacral spinal levels, and the pain is referred to the associated dermatomes. The pain associated with childbirth goes beyond the pain referred from the cervix and unfortunately is greater than that of a man-cold.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding urinary tract infections (UTIs) is FALSE?

options.html: UTIs are one of the most common reasons for patients presenting to primary care

Examples of first line antibiotic choices include nitrofurantoin and TMP/SMX

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Urine culture is unnecessary in typical simple UTIs. The causative agent is likely to be susceptible to a first-line antibiotic, so it is standard to immediately begin treatment with antibiotics. Urine culture will delay treatment and also increase unnecessary costs. If a UTI is repetitive, complicated, or more concerning, urine cultures is warranted.

weekLabel: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy
lectureMeta: Written fresh by the Meds 2025 volunteers in 2022. The bank states on its own second page that these were not verified by faculty.
stem: Which of the following statements regarding antibiotic use in UTIs is TRUE?

options.html: Septra (TMP/SMX) is the best option for UTIs because of low antimicrobial resistance
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is a benign condition that never requires treatment
Patients who experience recurrent UTIs can be given antibiotics prophylactically
Antibiotics are first line treatment for a patient with delirium
Male patients should always automatically receive IV antibiotics

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Prophylactic antibiotics are helpful for patients who have recurrent UTIs, which is defined as 2 or more uncomplicated UTIs within 6 months or 3 positive urine cultures within 12 months. Septra (TMP/SMX) is not as effective as some other antibiotics for treating UTIs because of increased antimicrobial resistance. Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not require treatment, but with some exceptions: pregnant patients and patients who are about to undergo urologic procedures. A patient with delirium should not be assumed to have a UTI; a thorough history should be taken to rule out other causes such as sensory impairment and a disruptive environment, and to avoid overtreatment with unnecessary antibiotics. Males should not always be considered to have complicated UTIs, and those with mild cases can begin with oral antibiotics.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of urinary retention?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Urinary retention is the inability to void urine. Kidney stones do not cause urinary retention because they do not block the passage of urine from the bladder out through the urethra.

stem: Which of the following statements about benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is FALSE?

options.html: Important points on patient history include dysuria, frequency, and nocturia
Digital rectal exam should be performed to assess for prostate size and nodularity
Patient quality of life due to urinary symptoms should be considered when assessing their need for BPH treatment
BPH is very common and affects over 50% of men over age 60
PSA is not helpful in the assessment of BPH

answer:
The correct answer is E.

PSA can be used as a surrogate marker of prostate size; larger prostates produce more PSA, which can be measured as elevated serum PSA levels. Serum PSA can be measured and compared over time to track prostate enlargement.

A man with a large prostate and severe LUTS that significantly impair his life should undergo radical prostatectomy
A man with a small prostate and severe LUTS that significantly impair his life should be given the option of α-blockers or surgery
A man with a large prostate and severe LUTS that do not cause him significant impairment should undergo surgery
A man with a small prostate and severe LUTS that do not cause him significant impairment should be given 5-α reductase inhibitors

The correct answer is C.

Refer to the CUA Guidelines for the Management of BPH Therapeutic Algorithm.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding prostate cancer screening is FALSE?

options.html: PSA screening should be discussed with all men over 50 years old
The role of PSA screening is controversial; North American and European guidelines differ
All men over the age of 70 should be offered a DRE and PSA screening
Prostate cancer screening does not require any imaging
PSA and DRE are used for screening; prostate cancer can only be definitively diagnosed with a prostate biopsy

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Men over the age of 70 are not offered routine screening for prostate cancer. This is because a diagnosis of prostate cancer would not change their management. By a similar line of thought, men with less than 10 years of life expectancy are not offered PSA screening.

stem: A 51M patient undergoes active surveillance for his low-risk prostate cancer. Unfortunately, his PSA doubling time has increased, suggesting that the tumor volume is progressing. The patient has ulcerative colitis and Lupus and refuses to have open surgery. Given this information, which of the following is the best management strategy?

options.html: Watchful waiting; do not initiate treatment
Insist that an open radical prostatectomy is the most appropriate management option
Help the patient decide between brachytherapy and laparoscopic prostatectomy
Help the patient decide between laparoscopic prostatectomy and external beam radiation
Help the patient decide between brachytherapy, laparoscopic prostatectomy, and external beam radiation

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This is a challenging question. An open radical prostatectomy does not align with the patient’s desire to avoid surgery. External beam radiation is not appropriate for patients with IBD or Lupus (or in this case, both!), as it can cause proctitis. Laparoscopic prostatectomy is a less invasive surgical option and should be offered. Brachytherapy is an excellent option as well.

stem: You are a radiologist. It is a lovely spring day and you are in a dark room reviewing a variety of images of renal masses. Which of the following radiological findings is most suggestive of renal cell carcinoma?

options.html: A single mass with smooth borders and solid elements
A small, exophytic solid mass that is strongly enhancing with contrast administration
A mildly enhancing, blood-filled mass with smooth borders and septa

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Options A and D are descriptions of renal cysts, which can be hyperdense (i.e. filled with blood or protein). Option C is an angiomyolipoma. Option B is most likely a renal cell carcinoma because it enhances brightly with contrast. However, this is not true in all cases.

options.html: Radical nephrectomy and ipsilateral adrenal gland removal

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A radical nephrectomy involves removing the kidney outside of Gerota’s fascia. This is a open surgery, and therefore, is not minimally invasive.

stem: You are a clinical clerk shadowing a urologist. Which of the following patients’ presentations is the most concerning for urinary tract cancer?

options.html: A 55F teacher with a 1-week history of lower urinary tract symptoms
A 22M mechanic with left flank pain, microscopic hematuria, and nausea and vomiting
A 71F hairdresser with gross, painless hematuria with stringy clots and back pain
A 74M truck driver with gross hematuria and BPH who takes anticoagulants for his atrial fibrillation

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Gross hematuria with stringy clots is a common finding in upper urinary tract cancer. Although males are at a slightly higher risk than females, the final patients presentation is more in keeping with his use of anticoagulation and previous diagnosis of BPH. This patient’s occupation as a hair dresser also places her at a higher risk of urogenital malignancy.

stem: On the second day of your family medicine rotation, you see a patient with gross hematuria. After a thorough history and physical exam, bladder cancer is at the top of your top differential diagnosis. What are your next steps? (Select all that apply)

options.html: Core needle biopsy of local lymph nodes
Bloodwork for a CBC, creatinine and electrolytes

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, D, F, I, J.

All of these investigations are part of the initial work up for suspected bladder cancer. Referral to a urologist is key; they will rule out benign causes and characterize malignant disease. A ureteroscopy, cystoscopy and core needle biopsy may be ordered by a urologist at a later time, if indicated. They are not part of the initial work up.

The correct answer is B.

Incontinence is a storage symptom. Voiding symptoms include: Weak stream, Intermittent voiding, Straining to void, Hesitancy, Emptying incompletely, Double voiding (WISHED). Storage symptoms include: Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia, and Incontinence.

stem: True or False: Thiazides commonly causes hypercalcemia.
answer:
The correct answer is B.

False. Although thiazide diuretics can be helpful in reabsorbing Ca2+ from urine back into bloodstream, it’s not a common cause of hypercalcemia. Other causes may include: hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, and sarcoidosis. Hypercalcemia causes polyuria, thirst, mental changes and renal failure.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Calcium phosphate stones precipitate in high urine pH. Uric stones and Cystine stones form in low urine pH – and thus therapeutic approach for uric and cystine stones include urinary alkalinization (raise urine pH!).

stem: In embryonic development, which pair of kidneys persists to become the adult kidneys?
answer: Answer D. This set of kidneys become the “permanent” kidneys in humans and is functional by 12 weeks of fetal development. They develop from the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesoderm. The Prenephros doesn’t exist, the pronephros degenerates by week 6 of development, and the mesonephros functions while the permanent kidneys develop. For more information, see the lecture “Development of the Urinary System”.

stem: Fanconi’s Syndrome is a disease of the kidney in which glucose, amino acids, uric acid, phosphate, and bicarbonate are passed into the urine instead of being reabsorbed. Where is the problem within the nephron?
answer: Answer B. The proximal tubule is where 50-60% of solutes and water are reabsorbed. Sodium moves down its concentration gradient and water moves along the osmotic gradient. Sodium moves into cells coupled with various substrates such as glucose and phosphate. The proximal tubule’s brush border also contains carbonic anhydrase which is important for bicarbonate reabsorption. The proximal tubule is also a key area for organic cation/anion secretion. For more information, see the lecture “A Trip Down the Tubule”.

stem: Where does the diuretic furosemide act within the nephron?

options.html: The proximal tubule at the Na+/glucose symporter
The thick ascending limb at the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter
The distal convoluted tubule at the Na+/Cl- symporter
The collecting duct principal cell at the passive Na+ channel

answer: Answer B. This is the site of action of loop diuretics such as furosemide. The thick ascending limb absorbs about 30% of filtered NaCl but no water. Furosemide acts such that less sodium, potassium, and chloride are reabsorbed and therefore more remains in the urine. For more information, see the lecture “A Trip Down the Tubule”.

stem: Where do thiazide diuretics act within the nephron?

options.html: The proximal tubule at the Na+/glucose symporter
The thick ascending limb at the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter
The distal convoluted tubule at the Na+/Cl- symporter
The collecting duct principal cell at the passive Na+ channel

answer: Answer C. Thiazides block the Na+/Cl- symporter. The distal convoluted tubule is important for reabsorbing more solute to make urine maximally dilute. When the symporter is blocked, the increased concentration of sodium in the lumen promotes the reabsorption of calcium through its channel. This results is decreased urinary calcium, which is important for patients with kidney stones. For more information, see the lecture “A Trip Down the Tubule”.

stem: Conn’s syndrome is the result of an aldosterone-producing adenoma. What would you expect in Conn’s syndrome (where there is an excess of aldosterone)?
answer: Answer E. Aldosterone is normally stimulated in response to decreased blood pressure and sodium concentration. Therefore, aldosterone increases the activity of the Na+/K+ ATPase, especially in the cortical collecting duct, increases the activity of principal cells and α-intercalated cells causing sodium retention, potassium secretion, and alkalosis. It also acts to increase the numbers and activity of sodium channels in the collecting ducts. Therefore, more sodium is retained while less potassium is retained in the presence of aldosterone. For more information, see the lecture “Sodium Handling in the Kidney”

stem: How does a physician estimate a patient’s total body sodium?
answer: Answer C. The diagnosis of total body sodium content is based on physical exam. No lab test will provide the answer. The sodium content of the body as a whole is not related to the serum level of sodium, instead it is a disorder of water handling (look at Dr. House’s two lectures on Sodium Handling in the body). A patient with high sodium content will have an elevated JVP, edema, ascites, and hypertension. A patient will have dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension, and a flat JVP is sodium content is low. For more information, see the lecture “Edema and Clinical Assessment of ECF Volume”.

stem: Which of the following statements about water handling and the kidney is true?

options.html: The excretion of a concentrated or dilute urine is determined primarily in the collecting tubules of the kidney
Antidiuretic hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary
In order to produce maximally dilute urine, ADH must be secreted by the posterior pituitary
If the body is producing too much ADH (such as in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), hypernatremia can result

answer: Answer A. Antidiuretic hormone is released from the posterior pituitary in response to increasing osmolarity as sensed by the hypothalamus and is inhibited by decreased osmolarity as sensed by the hypothalamus. ADH causes aquaporins to insert in the apical and basolateral membranes of the collecting tubule, primarily in the principal cells. B) is incorrect because ADH is produced by the posterior pituitary, C) is incorrect because in order to produce maximally dilute urine, ADH must be inhibited so that less water is reabsorbed. D) is incorrect because if there is too much ADH, hyponatremia would result from too much free water in the body.

stem: How many litres of isotonic saline do you need to infuse to get 1 litre of isotonic saline into the plasma?
answer: Answer D. There is a 2/3:1/4 relationship between the interstitial space and the vascular space, respectively. That means for every 1 L of normal saline you infuse, 3/4 ends up in the interstitial space and 1/4 ends up in the vascular space (plasma). Therefore, to get 1 L of normal saline into the plasma, you actually have to infuse 4 L.

stem: If you give someone 2 litres intravenous half normal saline, what amount of the 2 L will distribute intracellularly?
answer: Answer B. 2 L of half normal saline is the same as 1 L of normal saline mixed with 1 L of water. I L of normal saline will distribute in the interstitial fluid and vascular spaces but since it is isotonic will not distribute in the intracellular space. The 1 L of free water is hypotonic so it will distribute into the intracellular fluid as well as the extracellular fluid. Total body water is 2/3 intracellular and 1/3 extracellular. The 1 L of free water distributes according to this ratio, so 667 mL of free water will end up in the intracellular fluid.

stem: What is the antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
answer: Answer D. Fomepizole is given in cases of methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning. Activated charcoal is not very effective at absorbing alcohols so it is usually not indicated. Sodium bicarbonate can treat the metabolic acidosis (if the pH is dangerously low) but not the underlying cause of the metabolic acidosis (the toxic byproducts from methanol or ethylene glycol ingestion). Finally, flumazenil is the antidote for benzodiazepine poisoning (you will learn about it in the Emergency Care block). For more information, see the lecture “Acid- Base Physiology”.

stem: A teenager is brought to the emergency room after he was dared by his friends to hyperventilate until he fainted. If you had drawn and analyzed his blood gas when he fainted, what would you have seen?
answer: Answer B.He would have decreased carbon dioxide because he is hyperventilating, blowing more of it off. Because CO2 is decreased in the blood, less carbonic acid is combined with water to produce hydrogen ions in the blood. With decreased hydrogen ions, pH increases due to the inverse relationship with [H+] and pH. For more information, see the lecture “Acid-Base Physiology”.

stem: Francis, a 65-year-old man, was brought to the emergency room by his son who discovered him passed out in the garage. The following blood values were obtained: pH: 7.30 PCO2: 28 Na+: 141 K+: 4.6 HCO3-: 12 Cl-: 102 Osmolarity: 330 Glucose: 5 BUN: 7.1 What acid-base disorder does Francis have?
answer: Answer C. First, look at the pH given. It’s below normal (7.4) so we know it is an acidosis. In acidosis either PCO2 is high (greater than 40 mmHg—respiratory acidosis) or HCO3- is low (less than 24 mEq/L—metabolic acidosis). Looking at the given values, PCO2 is low so it is not a respiratory acidosis. However, his HCO3- is low, suggesting a metabolic acidosis. For more information, see the lecture “Acid-Base Physiology”.

stem: Did respiratory compensation occur? If so, was there full respiratory compensation?
answer: Answer A. In metabolic acidosis, acid gain or bicarbonate loss should result in a 1:1 equivalent reduction in PCO2 in healthy people with no other acid-base abnormalities. In this problem, the bicarbonate has decreased by 12 and his PCO2 has also decreased by 12. Therefore, respiratory compensation did occur as the expected reduction in the blood value for PCO2. stem: A 66-year-old man presents with polyuria, nocturia, intermittent headache, and fatigue. Her lab values are Cr 107, Na 178, K 1.5, Cl 109, HCO3 32, albumin 40. The resident orders an aldosterone:renin ratio and it comes back high. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The patient has hypokalemia and hypernatremia along with metabolic alkalosis. The key is in the aldosterone: renin ratio. A high ratio indicates an increase in aldosterone that’s not due to activation of the RAAS system. Therefore, Conn syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism due to an adrenal tumor is the only one that fits. All the other answers would not increase the aldosterone: renin ratio.

stem: A 53-year-old woman comes into the ER due to severe diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. She recently was on a cruise to the Caribbean. Her medications include: ramipril and spironolactone for her hypertension, crestor for her hypercholesterolemia, ibuprofen for her chronic back pain, and prophylactic heparin to prevent DVT (she has a positive history for recurrent DVTs). On investigation, her creatinine is 90, Na 143, K 2.0, Cl 111, HCO3 20, albumin 38. Which of the following contributed to her hypokalemia?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Diarrhea caused volume contraction leading to aldosterone secretion which led to acute K+ loss. ACEI/Spironolactone/NSAIDs all prevent K+ excretion (might lead to hyperkalemia). Cristor (a statin) has no significant effect on K+. In this case the acute and severe diarrhea PLUS vomiting caused her hypokalemia.

stem: Mr. Smith, a 57-year-old man comes into your office for his routine checkup. Your clinic is running a bit behind and you see him an hour after his scheduled time. Physical exam and lab investigations are all fine except for a serum potassium of 7.1. What is the most likely cause?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Since investigations are all normal, it is slightly odd to have such a high potassium level without changes in other values. The mostly likely cause is pseudohyperkalemia due to prolonged storage of the blood sample before measurement. Pseudohyperkalemia can also be seen in patients with white blood counts over 500 x109/L or platelet counts greater than 750 x 109/L.

stem: After insertion of the Foley catheter, you notice the patient’s urine output is 8L in 12 hours. This makes you concerned for:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

When someone has urinary retention for prolonged period of time and it is suddenly relieved, diuresis of the excess urea and water occurs. Rarely, it is possible to develop nephrogenic diabetes insipidus where the distal convoluted tubule does not respond to ADH. This leads to excessive loss of electrolytes, hypovolemia. To monitor this, hourly urine output must be monitored, along with BP. Electrolytes must be checked. The fluid loss can often be regained through drinking, however if that’s not enough, you can give IV normal saline.

stem: Camilla is 6 years old. Camilla’s mother brings her to the family doctor’s office because she has been having “accidents”. answer:
The correct answer is D.

Secondary diurnal enuresis – Nocturnal enuresis occurs solely at night while diurnal has adaytime component. Primary enuresis occurs if a child has never had a period without enuresis while secondary enuresis occurs after a 6 month dry period. Thus, Camilla has secondary diurnal enuresis.

stem: Which of the following are options in the management of nocturnal enuresis?

stem: Chelsea is a 77 year old woman with known SIADH from a brain lesion. Physical exam suggests she is euvolemic. Her electrolyte panel comes back as follows: Serum [Na+] 120 mmol/L Serum [K+] 4 mmol/L Serum Osm 270mOsm Urine Osm 600mOsm What is the apparent electrolyte imbalance and which IV fluids should we use to correct it?

options.html: Likely pseudohyponatremia from underlying diabetes – no IV fluids

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Reference range of serum [Na+] is 135-145mmol/L, serum [K+] is 3.5-5mmol/L, both are tightly regulated by the kidneys. The patient is hyponatremic due to SIADH since the kidney is bombarded by ADH and cannot effectively release water to the bladder, resulting in highly concentrated urine. Water is instead retained in her ECF thereby diluting her serum [Na+] causing hyponatremia – although her total body Na+ is normal by physical exam. The goal of IV fluids will be to allow her kidney to release water which will restore serum [Na+] to normal levels. A-No, the patient is hyponatremic. B-No, if we put in 300mOsm and the urine is 600mOsm then by C1V1=C2V2 the urine output will be 0.5L from adding 1L IV = +0.5 L ECF volume gain (opposite of what we wanted). C-Yes, if we add 1L of 1000mOsm fluid and urine output is 600mOsm then by C1V1=C2V2 she will pee out 2L, resulting in net -1L ECF volume (success!) this will in turn restore her serum [Na+]. D-No, the patient’s total body Na+ is normal (she is euvolemic), the problem is the concentration of Na+ not the total amount. E-Her serum Osm is actually low, in diabetes osmotically active glucose in the blood would inflate the serum Osm and cause apparent hyponatremia.

stem: A farmer is brought to the ER at 4AM after feeling dizzy, weak, palpitations, and deep unusual breathing. His blood labs are: pH = 7.10 pCO2 = 40 HCO3 = 12 Albumin = 30 Na = 140 K = 2.5 Cl = 102 What the least likely cause of the electrolyte imbalance?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The above stem is a case of metabolic acidosis since pH <7.35, pCO2 normal with reduced HCO3- . Anion gap is Na – HCO3 – Cl = 140-12-102 = 26. A normal anion gap is 12 with a deviation of 3 for every 10 difference in albumin from the reference value of 40. Since his albumin is 30, his expected anion gap is 9 to 15, therefore he has Anion gap metabolic acidosis. For AGMA we use the MUDPILES acronym to brainstorm possible causes. A-Possible, MeOH is the M of MUDPILES. B-Possible, DKA is the D of MUDPILES. C-Possible, Lactic Acidosis is the L of MUDPILES. D-Unlikely, diarrhea causes loss of HCO3- which would cause metabolic acidosis but would not generate an anion gap.

C-Urgent hemodialysis should always be considered for urgent electrolyte imbalances, especially when they do not respond to first line treatment. D-B Agonists also cause K+ to shift to the ICF. stem: A 70 year old woman with CKD stage IV experiences gradual loss of bone mass (beyond normal aging). She is diagnosed with osteitis fibrosa cystica – what are your first 3 therapy options? (Choose 3 options)

options.html: encourage outdoor exposure to natural sun

answer:
The correct answer is A, D, E.

Osteitis fibrosa cystica is a consequence of CKD. The kidneys play an important metabolic role in the conversion of inactivated Vitamin D (-25 OH) -> activated Vitamin D (1,25 OH) “calcitriol”. CKD causes low calcium and high phosphates, the body responds with parathyroid hormone (PTH) to transfer calcium from the bones to the blood. However bone breakdown also releases phosphate which leads to hyperphosphatemia. A – yes, this would reduce hyperphosphatemia. B – no, this would exacerbate hyperphosphatemia. C – no, this would further stimulate PTH. D – yes, this would reduce the activity of PTH. E – yes, this is the solution to the underlying pathology. F – this is unlikely to have much acute clinical benefit. G – not effective here. H – no role here since the absorption of calcium and phosphate happens in the small intestine not the colon. I- The thyroid produces calcitonin which actually works against PTH, removal would further exacerbate the hyperphosphatemia

stem: This class of diuretics is mainly used in patients with congestive heart failure or liver cirrhosis with ascites and edema
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Potassium sparing diuretics, such as spironolactone, eplerenone, triamterene, and amiloride, decrease excretion of potassium with diuresis. They act on the distal convoluted tubule and/or collecting duct. Spironolactone and eplerenone are used in patients with congestive heart failure or liver cirrhosis with ascites and edema, whereas triamterene and amiloride are not often prescribed.

stem: A 64-year-old male comes into your nephrology clinic referred by their family doctor. On a routine checkup, the family doc found 3+ proteinuria in the patient’s urine as well as hypoalbuminemia. The patient’s HPI is significant for donating one of his kidneys to a family member when he was 32. No other significant findings. You suspect he may have nephrotic syndrome. Would you biopsy his kidney?
answer: Answer B. Contraindications to renal biopsy include: - Solitary kidney - Uncooperative patient - Uncontrolled severe hypertension - Severe anemia - Cystic kidney - Hydronephrosis - Acute pyelonephritis - Multiple renal artery aneurysms - Renal neoplasm - End stage renal failure

stem: A 67-year-old female with a history of recent shigella infection was given gentamicin. Recent labs show BUN 8, Cr 175, and brown muddy casts in her urine. What is the most appropriate treatment for her condition?
answer: Answer D. This lady has nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis. The treatment is to stop the offending cause (the aminoglycoside) and rehydrate her. answer: Answer D.Low GFR is a sign of chronic kidney disease or acute renal impairment. stem: Which of the following is NOT a specific treatment for treating renal disease progression?
answer: Answer D. NSAIDs (except ASA)can actually increase the progression of chronic kidney disease as well as interfere with the effectiveness of other drugs. The mechanism of this is primarily hemodynamic. Prostaglandins cause vasodilation of the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli, maintaining adequate perfusion. NSAIDs inhibit the production of prostaglandins, causing vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles and subsequent hypo-perfusion leading to further kidney damage.

stem: Which of the following is considered the gold standard for detecting proteinuria?
answer: Answer A. 24 hour urine collection is the most accurate measure because it takes into account GFR changes and other factors that can cause protein excretion to fluctuate during the day or in a single sample. Although it is the gold standard, a urinalysis is the better screening test because 24-hr urine collection is time consuming and tedious.

answer: Answer E. Hematuria is not found in diabetic nephropathy, the pathologic changes cause proteinuria and decline in GFR. Incidence of diabetic nephropathy is higher in patients with a history of poorly managed diabetes.

stem: Which of the following statements about microscopic hematuria is FALSE?

options.html: It may have benign causes like menstruation, vigorous exercise, sexual activity, viral illness or urinary tract infections.
An individual with microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts, dysmorphia and elevated serum creatinine should be evaluated for primary renal disease.
If no benign causes for microscopic hematuria are found and the patient has a normal urinalysis and renal function then the patient does not need further investigation.
Certain medications like aminoglycosides, cyclophosphamide, and diuretics can cause microscopic hematuria.
Microscopic hematuria is defined as ≥ 2 RBC/hpf on 2 separate urinalyses without recent exercise, menses, sexual activity or instrumentation.

answer: Answer C. The patient described here should have a referral to urology to further examine the cause of their hematuria. All other statements are true.

stem: Which of the following statements is true about kidney disease in children.

options.html: Compared to adults, children have a much lower incidence of chronic kidney disease.
Compared to adults, children have a much higher incidence of acquired renal disease.
Compared to adults, children have a much lower incidence of abnormalities of the urinary tract.
The incidence of chronic kidney disease in children is falling.

answer: Answer A. Children have a lower incidence of chronic kidney disease, a lower incidence of acquired kidney disease and a higher incidence of abnormalities of the urinary tract when compared to adults. More than half of patients seen by paediatric nephrologists have congenital renal disease or abnormalities of the urinary tract. The incidence of chronic kidney disease in children is rising (though it is still less than the incidence in adults).

stem: When diagnosing nephrotic syndrome in children, when is a biopsy performed?

options.html: After 28 days if the symptoms haven’t resolved.
Upon presentation before treatment is initiated.
Upon presentation, immediately before starting the child on corticosteroids and then changing or eliminating the corticosteroids if needed.
If there is no response after treatment with corticosteroids for 28 days.
You do not need to perform a biopsy in children, nephrotic syndrome is always due to minimal change disease which responds well to corticosteroids.

answer: Answer D. Minimal change disease is so common (70-90%) and exquisitely steroid sensitive that you treat with corticosteroids for 28 days before doing a biopsy. 28 days is based on the maximal sensitivity and specificity of time to remission.

stem: Which of the following tests is recommended for calculating GFR in children?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Cystatin C is a base proteinase inhibitory with a low molecular weight that is freely filtered through the glomerulus and only the glomerulus, is not secreted, and is not influenced by many other factors that do affect creatinine. Creatinine is only reduced once kidney function in children has declined by 50% and must be corrected for height. Cystatin C has been shown to be superior to creatinine for detecting chronic kidney disease early.

stem: Which of the following is the least appropriate way to estimate GFR of a pediatric patient?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

A – Creatinine is not perfect (its secreted by the proximal tubule) but its standard and decent if used with MDRD or CDK Epi formulas. B – Cystatin C is the current best pediatric marker. C – BUN is generally less accurate than creatinine (BUN has many confounding metabolic and physiologic processes). D – Radiotracers which are neither absorbed nor secreted by the tubules can be highly accurate. E – 24h urine if done properly can be used to derive the renal clearance by first principles

stem: Henry has an eGFR of 42, which stage of chronic kidney failure does her fall into? Is he at risk for irreversible progression?

The correct answer is D.

CKD is classified as 5 stages: I – GFR >90 II – GFR is 60-89 III – GFR is 30-59 IV – GFR is 15-29 V – GFR <15 Once at stage 3, the patient is at risk for irreversible progression of their renal impairment.

stem: Which of the following is true about diabetic nephropathy?

options.html: Pre-existing low GFR is not a risk factor for diabetic nephropathy
Patients with microalbuminuria have a low change to progress to overt proteinuria
Guidelines suggests start ACEI / ARB at BP of 140/90 for diabetic patients
Start screening for diabetic nephropathy in type 1 diabetic patients 5 years after original diabetes diagnosis
A renal biopsy is required to diagnose diabetic nephropathy

answer:
The correct answer is D.

A – False, low GFR is a risk factor for diabetic nephropathy. B – False, microalbuminuria has a 50% chance to progress to overt proteinuria on average. C – False, start ACEI/ARB for BP of 130/80. D – True, since we can be fairly certain of the onset for type 1 diabetes (unlike type 2 which often has unknown timeline) we can save the healthcare system unnecessary burden by starting screening at 5 years. E – Renal biopsies are rarely done for diabetic nephropathy, they are sometimes done for renal cancer however

stem: Mr. G is a type 1 diabetic who is worried about developing diabetic nephropathy. His HgBA1C is 6%, his blood pressure is 140/80, and his LDL is 1.8. Considering the treatment goals for patient with diabetes with respect to preventing progression of renal disease, which treatment goal has he not yet accomplished?

options.html: He has not achieved the targeted HgBA1C
He has not achieved the targeted blood pressure
He has not achieved the targeted LDL
He has achieved all the treatment targets to prevent progression of renal disease

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Treatment targets for diabetics are: • Tight glycemic control: target HgB A1C <7% • Tight blood pressure control: target BP < 130/80 • Right control of hyperlipidemia: target LDL <2 Mr. G has not met the targeted blood pressure. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are medications of choice because they help reduce intraglomerular pressure as they vasodilate the efferent arteriole.

stem: True or False: Type 2 diabetics should be screened for diabetic nephropathy starting at the time of diagnosis, whereas type 1 diabetics should be screened for diabetic nephropathy starting 5 years after the diagnosis.
answer: True. Diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes may be late in disease progression because insulin resistance builds gradually, and symptoms appear gradually. Therefore, type 2 diabetics need to be screened immediately for diabetic nephropathy as they may already be late in disease progression. Type 1 diabetes will have immediate symptoms (without insulin, your body cannot function normally), so their diagnosis is very early in disease progression.

application.

stem: This class of diuretics are widely used for the treatment of hypertension and to prevent cardiovascular events
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Thiazide diuretics, including thiazide type diuretics (chlorothiazide and hydrochlorothiazide) and thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide, and metolazone), are widely used for the treatment of hypertension and to prevent cardiovascular events. They act on the distal convoluted tubule by blocking the NA-CL symporter to increase excretion of Na+ and Cl-.

stem: This class of diuretics are often given to patients with high intra-cranial pressure in emergency settings such as a brain bleed to quickly bring down that pressure
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Osmotic diuretics, including glycerine, urea, and mannitol, act on segments of the nephron that are freely permeable to water such as the proximal convoluted tubule and the thin ascending loop of Henle. They quickly increase the osmolarity of renal filtrate to increase urine volume.

stem: This class of diuretics are used in both inpatient and outpatient settings when patients are ECF volume expanded, for example, due to congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, or liver cirrhosis
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Loop diuretics, such as furosemide (Lasix) and ethacrynic acid act on the thick ascending loop of Henle by blocking the NA-K-2Cl transporter so more sodium, potassium, and chloride get excreted. They cause the most sodium excretion of all diuretics and can increase diuresis even in patients who are responding maximally to other diuretics

stem: A 76-year-old male presents to his GP with obstructive urinary symptoms. A palpable nodule is found in his prostate on DRE and he is referred to a urologist for a biopsy that finds malignancy of Gleason score 8. What is the next step in management of this patient?

Referral to surgeon for radical prostatectomy
Begin hormone therapy and reassess in 3 months

answer: Answer A. CT scan is needed to assess local spread. It would be important to visualize local lymph nodes and organs for any metastases that may be present. answer: Answer B. This patient is eligible for radiation salvage therapy as he is likely to recover and has no evidence of systemic metastases from his cancer. Surgery is rarely repeated and hormone therapy is primarily used when there is metastatic recurrence.

stem: Where does transitional cell carcinoma most commonly occur?
answer: Answer A. Transitional cell carcinoma is the most common type of genitourinary tract cancer and most commonly affects the bladder, possibly due to the link between carcinogens in the urine and transitional cell carcinoma (urine spends the most amount of time in the bladder).

stem: A 19-year-old male presents to the emergency room with sudden onset of severe pain in his left testicle. On exam the left testicle is hard and extremely tender to palpation. There is no fever, nausea, or vomiting present. What is the most likely diagnosis and its corresponding treatment
answer: Answer D. The presentation is most consistent with testicular torsion due to the age of the patient, sudden onset, lack of other symptoms and findings on physical exam. This is a surgical emergency due to the lack of blood supply when the spermatic cord becomes twisted. Delays of a few hours may significantly decrease the success rate of salvaging the testicle.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of his right testicle. On exam you find a firm nodule about 0.5cm in size. The patient is experiencing no systemic symptoms and found the mass during a self-check. His father and brother both have a history of testicular cancer. What is the most appropriate next step for this patient?
answer: Answer E. Ultrasound is the most appropriate next step to examine for presence of solid masses in the testicle when testicular cancer is suspected. It is useful to help characterize the mass as cystic ones are benign in nature. Baseline chest x-ray and chest/abdo CT scans can be done later to look for metastases. A radical orchiectomy could be done later if the suspicion of cancer is higher after ultrasound and serum markers (aFP, bHCG, LDH) are completed.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with repeated microscopic hematuria. There are no significant findings on physical exam. He has a history of tobacco use and has worked in a tire factory for 36 years. All measures of kidney function are normal and no casts are found on urinalysis. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
answer: Answer B. This patient is at risk for bladder cancer. Painless hematuria is the most common presentation. Transitional cell carcinoma is most common with peak incidence between 50 and 60 years old. Males are affected twice as often as females. Exposure to cigarette smoke and tire manufacturing processes are possible factors in the pathogenesis. Flexible cystoscopy is mandatory in the workup of suspected bladder tumors and allows you to see flat lesions that may occur in transitional cell carcinoma which are not visible on CT or other imaging modalities. Retrograde urethrogram evaluates for urethral injury while CT is performed for staging. Another useful investigation is an IVP which shows filling defect in the collecting system.

stem: Jim is a 55 year old male who works as a pilot for overnight cargo runs. He is active playing golf with his friends and he maintains a healthy lifestyle. Additionally, he is followed by his family doctor who reports he is up to date on all recommended cancer screenings. He never smokes and drinks socially. Over the past 6 months he noticed difficulty voiding. He reports weak stream, increased frequency/urgency, and feeling of incomplete emptying. He occasionally reports having to get up at night to go pee. His physical exam, including a DRE were all unremarkable What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

A – unlikely, also does not have important smoking risk factor. B – this would cause him to urinate less and result in highly concentrated urine which is not described here. C – most likely, stem mentions several FUNWISE symptoms, typical demographic group – DRE can often be negative for mild/moderate BPH, especially without skilled examiner. D – Unlikely, would consider this in an older gentleman with hematuria or family history. E – unlikely. Diabetes can lead to excess glucose in the tubules which drags water with it resulting in increased urination. However, weak stream and incomplete emptying suggest more of a mechanical problem (partial obstruction) than just too much urine. Furthermore, he has presumably been screened recently for diabetes and has an active lifestyle to control his blood sugar.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with severe testicular pain. Upon physical examination the patient’s testicles are very hard. The physician suspects testicular torsion and orders a doppler ultrasound. Which of the following are the expected results of the scan and the appropriate treatment if positive for testicular torsion?

options.html: Increased blood flow to the testicles, antibiotic treatment
Impaired blood flow to the testicles, antibiotic treatment
Increased blood flow to the testicles, surgical treatment
Impaired blood flow to the testicles, surgical treatment

answer:
The correct answer is D.

If the patient has testicular torsion we can expect to see impaired blood flow to the testicles. Testicular torsion requires surgical treatment. If the patient were suspected to have epididymitis, we would likely see increased blood flow to the testicles and this would require antibiotic treatment (for the infection).

Patient need to be informed about risks and benefits of screening in order to make an informed decision
PSA and DRE should be offered for men aged 50-69
For men who are at an increased risk, screening is recommended starting at 45 years old
All of these statements about prostate cancer screening are true

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Prostate cancer screening recommendations: • Discuss issues regarding prostate cancer screening with men over 50 years old • Patients need to be informed about risks and benefits of screening in order to make an informed decision • If a patient decides to be screened, ffer PSA and DRE for men age 50/55-69 years every 2 years. No routine screening for men age 40-50/54 years. No screening for men age > 70 years. No screening if life expectancy < 10 years. For men who are at an increased risk, it is recommended to start screening at age 45

stem: A patient presents to your family clinic with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following correctly lists obstructive symptoms of BPH?

options.html: Straining, slow stream, sensation of incomplete emptying

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Obstructive symptoms of BPH include slow stream, hesitancy, post void dribbling, sensation of incomplete emptying, straining. Irritative symptoms of BPH include urgency/urgency incontinence, nocturia, and frequent urination. Obstructive symptoms tend to occur early in the disease progression and irritative symptoms tend to occur later due to the bladder chronically working against obstruction.

stem: What is the most common type of renal stone?
answer: Answer D. Calcium oxalate is the most common type and comprises 80% of stones, uric acid accounts for 15% of stones, struvite (or magnesium ammonium phosphate) accounts for 4% and cystine accounts for 1%.

stem: Which of the following dietary factors predisposes to kidney stones?
answer: Answer E. Although it was previously thought that high calcium intake predisposes to kidney stones, it has been found that low calcium actually predisposes to kidney stones because oxalate is not bound in the gut with a low calcium intake. Low fluid intake, low calcium intake, low potassium intake, high salt intake and high protein intake are predisposing factors in order of descending importance.

stem: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 3 hour history of severe pain in his left flank radiating to the abdomen and down to his groin. He has and 2 similar episodes of passed renal stones in the last few years. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Wait until the stone passes and advise dietary changes and weight loss to prevent future occurrences.
Attempt to identify the stones by looking at urine crystals and KUB x-ray.
Investigate with urinalysis, urine pH and specific gravity, urine culture and sensitivity, and, blood tests (calcium, uric acid, bicarbonate, PTH)

answer: Answer D. Recurrent stones are a cause for investigation.B and C are both appropriate steps in the initial investigation of kidney stones. Predisposing factors are idiopathic hypercalciuria, hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypociraturia

stem: A 40-year-old female presents to the emergency department with fever, right flank pain, nausea, and vomiting. Renal ultrasound shows a right-side staghorn calculus. Which organism is the most likely cause of this patient’s kidney stone?
answer: Answer B. Proteus is a urease produce organism. Urease in the urine causes the production of ammonia which raises the pH of the urine and leads to phosphate precipitation. This leads to magnesium ammonium calcium phosphate stones (struvite), which more commonly cause staghorn calculi than other types of kidney stones. These often present in combination with UTIs due to Proteus, Pseudomonas, or Klebsiella.

stem: In which of the following cases of renal stones are you least likely to remove the stone surgically?

options.html: A 32-year-old woman with a 15 years history of poorly managed type I diabetes.
A 41-year-old man with a 2mm stone that was found incidentally.
A 45-year-old pilot with no significant medical history.
A 36-year-old man with severe, unremitting pain that has lasted for 10 hours.
A 40-year-old woman with a fever and history of frequent urination.

answer: Answer B. Most stones (70%) pass on their own without intervention. All of the other cases include an indication for surgery. Poorly controlled diabetes is a risk factor for renal dysfunction. Certain occupations indicate surgery due to the inability to safely pass a stone (i.e. bus drivers, pilots, etc.). Severe unremitting pain is an indication that the stone is not passing well on its own. Fever and frequent urination indicate a potential UTI.

stem: Which of the following is a drawback to peritoneal dialysis?

options.html: Patient survival is worse with peritoneal dialysis.
Peritoneal dialysis is more expensive than hemodialysis
Peritoneal dialysis cannot be done at home.
There is a higher rate of technique failure with peritoneal dialysis.

answer: Answer E. there is a higher rate of technique failure compared to hemodialysis. stem: Eduardo is a 65 year old type 1 diabetic with severe chronic renal failure (GFR of 6) that is managed by his nephrologist. He also is known to have severe pancreatic issues for which he is managed by his endocrinologist and family doctor. He has good social support at home and his wife helps drive him to his appointments. He is known to have type O+ blood and has never received transplant of any organs before. General workup shows 35% panel reactive antibodies to his wife’s HLA markers with high PRA score. Which of the following would NOT be an appropriate potential treatment option for this patient with respect to his CKD?

options.html: Joint kidney and pancreases transplant from a deceased donor
Kidney transplant from his wife, who is also O+ blood type
In clinic hemodialysis 3 times a week

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Given his GFR<7, good social supports, and lack of previous transplants he is a potential kidney transplant recipient. A – Type 1 (not type 2) diabetics are possibly eligible for this rare surgery which if successful would cure his diabetes and his renal failure. B – Living donors are associated with better results than deceased donors however he has a high concentration of anti-HLA antibodies to his wife – an absolute contraindication for transplant (the graft would be rejected). C – Home dialysis is possible and would save the couple many visits to the dialysis clinic. D – If the couple does not comfortable with peritoneal dialysis, in clinic dialysis is the most common option. E – Any patient with multiple organ end stage disease should always be considered for possible palliative care

stem: Which of the following is NOT an urgent indication for dialysis?

options.html: Uncontrollable hyperkalemia, acidosis, or fluid overload

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Sudden onset arrythmia is not an indication for dialysis. Urgent indications for dialysis include convulsions/coma/confusion, neuropathy, pericarditis, progressive malnutrition, uncontrollable hyperkalemia/acidosis/fluid overload. Relative indications for dialysis include severe uremic symptoms not relieved by conservative management (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, severe pruritis), or GFR<6mL/min.

stem: A 72 year old man lives with his wife and son. He is a retired truck driver who is obese (BMI 38) with poor diet and smokes regularly – ½ pack per day, 30 year history. His known allergies include penicillin and shellfish. His medications have not been changed recently by his family doctor, they include Ramipril, Atorvastatin, and Metoprolol. He states he is a social drinker – 4 beers a week and denies any drug use. His medical records indicate his pre-existing renal impairment (Creatinine baseline of 125). He also had previous TURP surgery for BPH 8 years ago. Recently he had severe crushing chest pain while shoveling snow. He was rushed to the ER where his cardiac situation was resolved with angiogram with IV contrast and a coronary artery stent. In the hospital 3 days later his creatinine shoots up to 200. He also develops pneumonia which is suspected by chest CT which is otherwise unremarkable – it is treated by gentamycin. The next day he looks like he may require ICU admission. As the internal medicine consult you are called to assess the patient – all other hospital investigations were unremarkable. His vitals taken upon ER admission were: BP: 130/80 HR 110 RR: 20 O2 Sat: 95% T: 37.2 What are your 4 most reasonable sources of kidney injury for this patient? (Choose 4 options)

options.html: Chronic Kidney failure from undiagnosed diabetes
Kidney metastasis from undiagnosed lung cancer
Cholesterol emboli from cardiac catheter to kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is C, E, F, G.

A – Although rhabdomyolysis can cause elevated GFR acutely, the patient has no symptoms consistent with this. B – CKD would almost never cause a spike in creatinine as seen in the scenario. C – possible, many patients with CKD are susceptible to AKI from IV contrast . D – highly unlikely, the chest CT for his pneumonia did not show any lung primary malignant mass. E – likely, Gentamycin is notorious for causing AKI. F – possible, the risk of this catastrophic event is roughly 1% for cardiac catheterizations. G – possible, although his vitals upon admission were reasonable, his cardiac event may have caused renal ischemia. H – unlikely, although a possible cause of post renal AKI, the patient has no symptoms consistent with kidney stones.
